title: Before I Formed You in the Womb
subtitle: Jeremiah 1
description: A boy from Anathoth is told he was known before he was formed, and is given a commission with two halves: uproot and plant.
paragraphs: Jeremiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a small town in the territory of Benjamin, a short walk from Jerusalem. The word of the LORD first came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, and it kept coming for the rest of his life, through the reign of Jehoiakim and all the way to the fifth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year, when the people of Jerusalem went into exile. He did not apply for the work. By the time it reached him, God said, it had already been settled before he was born.

The call itself leaves no room to negotiate. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations.” Jeremiah answered the way a young man answers when the assignment is bigger than he is. He said he did not know how to speak, that he was only a child. God refused the excuse outright. He told Jeremiah not to call himself a child, because the sending would decide where he went and the commanding would decide what he said. “For to everyone I send you, you must go, and all that I command you, you must speak. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you.”

Then the LORD reached out His hand and touched Jeremiah's mouth. “Behold, I have put My words in your mouth. See, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant.” Count the verbs and you have the shape of the man's whole life. Four of them tear down. Two of them build. Most of what Jeremiah would say for the next forty years would be uprooting and destroying, spoken to kings and priests and people who had every reason to silence him, and the planting would mostly be promised to a generation he would not live to see.

God gave him two pictures to carry. The first was a branch of an almond tree, the tree that wakes earliest in the year, and when Jeremiah named it, God answered, “You have observed correctly,” and added, “for I am watching over My word to accomplish it.” The second picture was darker. “I see a boiling pot,” Jeremiah said, “and it is tilting toward us from the north.” The meaning came with it. “Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land.” Kings from the north would set their thrones at the gates of Jerusalem, and the judgment would not be an accident of politics. God named its cause plainly: His people had forsaken Him and worshiped the works of their own hands.

The commission ends with a command to stand and a promise to hold him up. “Get yourself ready. Stand up and tell them everything that I command you.” God made him, that day, “like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land,” against its kings, its officials, its priests, and its people. The resistance was not a possibility. It was part of the appointment. “They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you.” Jeremiah was going to need every word of that promise, and the book that follows is the record of how often he nearly did not survive the needing of it.

title: The Fountain of Living Water
subtitle: Jeremiah 2
description: Israel is charged with two evils in one act: forsaking the fountain of living water, and hewing out broken cisterns that hold nothing.
paragraphs: The first sermon Jeremiah preaches in this book is a lawsuit, and it opens with a wedding memory. God tells him to proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem, “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.” Israel had once followed God into a desert with nothing in it, trusting Him for food and direction. That was the beginning of the relationship. The sermon exists because of how far the present stands from it.

God puts the question that starts the case. “What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me? They followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves.” Nobody in the chain of leadership escapes it. “The experts in the law no longer knew Me, and the leaders rebelled against Me. The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed useless idols.” Then God points outward, to Cyprus and to Kedar, to the far west and the far east, and asks whether anything like this has ever happened anywhere. “Has a nation ever changed its gods? (Yet they are not gods at all.) But My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols.” Other nations stay loyal to gods that are not gods at all. Israel traded the real God away.

The charge comes down to two acts, and Jeremiah gives them in God's words. “For My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns.” The cisterns were the replacement, human work meant to store what God gave freely and constantly, and they failed at the one thing a cistern is for. They were “broken cisterns that cannot hold water.” You can see the same reaching in the nation's politics, running to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile and to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates, as if safety could be imported. God's verdict on all of it is a sentence Jeremiah will repeat for forty years in different forms. “Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?”

What makes the sermon cut is that the people do not think they have done anything. God had planted them, He says, “like a choice vine from the very best seed,” and asks, “How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?” But when He names the running after other gods, the answer comes back as a denial. She insists, “I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals.” And when the pursuit itself is described, a young she-camel galloping here and there, a wild donkey sniffing the wind in her desire, the people do not repent of it. They settle into it. “It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, and I must go after them.”

The sermon ends in the courtroom. Judah's gods, God says, are as numerous as her cities, one for every town, and He invites them to do the saving. “But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can; for your gods are as numerous as your cities, O Judah.” Underneath it all sits the claim that the judgment will answer. The people keep saying, “I am innocent. Surely His anger will turn from me.” They keep saying, “I have not sinned.” God's reply is that He will judge them precisely for saying it. The first step back, as the next sermon will show, is the one word this people will not say.

title: Return, O Faithless Children
subtitle: Jeremiah 3
description: The call to return runs through the chapter like a refrain, while the north is summoned home and the valley fills with what Israel has loved.
paragraphs: The sermon opens with a law everyone in the audience knew. If a man divorces his wife and she marries another man, he can never take her back. The land itself would be defiled by it. God states the rule only to break past it with a question. Israel has not had one other husband. “But you have played the harlot with many lovers,” He says, “and you would return to Me?” The question hangs there unanswered, because the rest of the chapter is God answering it Himself, and His answer is yes, if she will come.

Before the invitation comes the evidence, and it comes through two sisters. In Josiah's days God walked Jeremiah through the comparison. The northern kingdom, faithless Israel, had run to every high hill and every green tree, and God had finally given her a certificate of divorce and sent her away. Her sister Judah watched the whole collapse happen. “Yet in spite of all this, her unfaithful sister Judah did not return to Me with all her heart, but only in pretense.” That is the verdict that shocks the sermon into motion. The sister who returned in pretense is judged worse than the sister who never pretended. “Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than unfaithful Judah.”

So the call goes out, of all places, toward the north, to the divorced sister, the one with no claim left. “Return, O faithless Israel.” And with it comes a promise about the face of God. “I will no longer look on you with anger, for I am merciful.” “I will not be angry forever.” The door is not opened by a payment or a pilgrimage or a season of better behavior. It is opened by one act of honesty. “Only acknowledge your guilt, that you have rebelled against the LORD your God.” The guilt is not in question. Confessing it is the whole price of return.

Inside the call, God lets Jeremiah see what the return grows into. “Return, O faithless children,” He says, “for I am your master, and I will take you,” gathering them, “and bring you to Zion.” “Then I will give you shepherds after My own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.” And then the sermon says something nobody expected about the most sacred object in the nation's life. In those days, God says, “they will no longer discuss the ark of the covenant of the LORD. It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made.” The ark would not be missed, because Jerusalem itself would carry the name. “At that time they will call Jerusalem The Throne of the LORD.” And the two broken halves of the people would walk together again. “In those days the house of Judah will walk with the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north to the land that I gave to your fathers as an inheritance.”

The sermon closes by speaking the answer before the people have given it, as if to teach them the words. God calls first. “Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.” Then the people's voice follows, rehearsed and ready for the day they mean it. “Here we are. We come to You, for You are the LORD our God.” And the confession the whole chapter has been asking for arrives in full at the end. “Let us lie down in our shame; let our disgrace cover us. We have sinned against the LORD our God, both we and our fathers; from our youth even to this day we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God.”

title: Disaster from the North
subtitle: Jeremiah 4
description: The foe from the north is named, the watchmen cry out, and Jeremiah sees creation itself run backward over his people.
paragraphs: The call to return is still open at the head of this sermon, and it comes with farm work attached. “If you will return, O Israel, return to Me,” God says, and then He talks about ground that has never been plowed. “Break up your unplowed ground, and do not sow among the thorns.” The outward mark of the covenant is not enough anymore. “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, O men of Judah and people of Jerusalem.” The sermon holds the door open with one hand. With the other, it is already sounding the alarm.

For the disaster Jeremiah saw in his first vision, the pot tilting from the north, is now close enough to describe. Blow the ram's horn through the land. Raise the signal flag toward Zion and run for the fortified cities. “A lion has gone up from his thicket, and a destroyer of nations has set out. He has left his lair to lay waste your land.” When that day comes, God says, the king and the officials will lose their courage, the priests will tremble, and the prophets will be astounded. The men whose job was to read the times will be the most surprised people in the city.

Jeremiah cannot stay inside the announcement, and this sermon is where his arguing with God first breaks the surface. The false prophets have been promising peace, and Jeremiah throws their promise back at heaven. He charges that God has deceived this people and Jerusalem by saying, “You will have peace,” and his reason is the present tense of the invasion: “while a sword is at our throats.” Then the vision takes him over completely, and the herald becomes a casualty of his own news. “My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh, the pain in my chest! My heart pounds within me; I cannot be silent.” He has heard the horn and the alarm of battle, and the sound is inside his body now. Disaster after disaster is proclaimed, and the tents of his own people are destroyed in a moment.

Then Jeremiah is shown the land as God sees it, and the vision runs creation backward. “I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void; I looked to the heavens, and they had no light.” The mountains quake. “I looked, and no man was left; all the birds of the air had fled.” “I looked, and the fruitful land was a desert.” Everything Genesis built up is taken down in four glances: no light, no people, no birds, no fruit. The world the sermon describes is not damaged. It is unmade.

But the unmaking has a border, and God states it in the middle of the vision. “The whole land will be desolate, but I will not finish its destruction.” Total, and yet not total. The sermon ends with the city still trying to dress for her lovers, painting her eyes and putting on scarlet and gold while the men she adorned herself for hunt her life. And the last sound in the chapter is not the horn. It is a woman in labor, the Daughter of Zion gasping for breath and stretching out her hands, crying, “Woe is me, for my soul faints before the murderers!”

title: If You Can Find a Single Person
subtitle: Jeremiah 5
description: God offers to pardon the city for one honest person, and Jeremiah reports what his search of the streets found.
paragraphs: The sermon begins as a search, and the terms are generous to the point of embarrassment. “Go up and down the streets of Jerusalem. Look now and take note; search her squares. If you can find a single person, anyone who acts justly, anyone who seeks the truth, then I will forgive the city.” One person. Not a righteous majority, not a remnant worth counting. One just person in the squares of Jerusalem, and the whole city is forgiven. The search fails at street level first. The people swear by the LORD's name and swear falsely in the same breath, and when God struck them, they felt nothing. “They have made their faces harder than stone and refused to repent.”

Jeremiah tries to excuse the failure before he accepts it. These are only the poor, he reasons. They do not know any better. He will go to the powerful, the people with standing, who surely know the way of the LORD and the justice of their God. What he finds at the top is the same ruin with better clothes. “But they too, with one accord, had broken the yoke and torn off the chains.” There is no class in the city that the rot has skipped. So the beasts of the earlier sermon are loosed in earnest: a lion from the forest, a wolf from the desert, a leopard lying in wait by the cities, because the rebellious acts are many.

Against all of this, the city has a theology, and Jeremiah quotes it so it can be answered. The people have lied about the LORD and said, “He will not do anything; harm will not come to us; we will not see sword or famine.” The prophets are only wind, they say. There is no word in them. God's answer to that sentence becomes Jeremiah's job description. “Because you have spoken this word, I will make My words a fire in your mouth and this people the wood it consumes.” And even here, in the chapter of the failed search, the border from the last sermon holds. “Yet even in those days,” God declares, “I will not make a full end of you.”

The sermon lingers on a contrast Jeremiah cannot get past. God set the sand as the boundary of the sea, “an enduring barrier it cannot cross,” and the waves surge and roar and obey it. The sea keeps its limit. God's people will not keep theirs. Their hearts are stubborn and rebellious, and the rains that come in season have been diverted by their own sins. Worse, the city is full of men who hunt people the way fowlers hunt birds, setting traps for men, filling their houses with deceit the way cages fill with birds, growing fat and sleek on it. And the charge God presses hardest is not about idols. “They have not taken up the cause of the fatherless, that they might prosper; nor have they defended the rights of the needy.”

The chapter ends with God naming the thing that has happened in the land as horrible and shocking, and then describing the arrangement everyone has agreed to live under. “The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority. My people love it so, but what will you do in the end?” It is the sermon's last line and its sharpest. The prophets lie because the people love the lie. The priests rule on their own authority because nobody asks for God's. The whole system works, right up until the end it refuses to think about, and God leaves the question standing in the street where the search began.

title: Rejected Silver
subtitle: Jeremiah 6
description: The bellows blow and the lead is spent, but the wicked are not drawn off; the LORD names them rejected silver.
paragraphs: The alarm Jeremiah sounded in the north now has a return address. Run for cover, sons of Benjamin. Sound the ram's horn in Tekoa, raise the signal over Beth-haccherem, because the disaster is close enough to name the towns it passes. Around Jerusalem the enemy is already camping like shepherds with their flocks, every man tending his own stretch of wall, and their voices carry over it. “Rise up, let us attack by night and destroy her fortresses!” God Himself gives the besiegers their engineering orders. “Cut down the trees and raise a siege ramp against Jerusalem. This city must be punished; there is nothing but oppression in her midst.” And the reason stands in the next verse like a spring that will not run clean. “As a well gushes its water, so she pours out her evil.”

Jeremiah's crisis in this sermon is that nobody is listening, and he says so to God's face. Their ears are closed. The word of the LORD has become offensive to them; they find no pleasure in it. Meanwhile the wrath is building in the prophet faster than he can hold it. “But I am full of the LORD’s wrath; I am tired of holding it back.” The sermon names what the whole city runs on, top to bottom. “For from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit.” And the religious treatment for a mortal wound is a bandage and a slogan. They dress the wound of God's people “with very little care.” Their cry is, “Peace, peace,” and the text answers it flatly: “when there is no peace at all.”

Shame might have saved them, and shame is gone. “Are they ashamed of the abomination they have committed? No, they have no shame at all; they do not even know how to blush.” So God sets the oldest offer in the book in front of them one more time, an offer shaped like a road. “Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths.” “Then walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls.” The whole sermon turns on what the people say next, and they say it in five words. “We will not walk in it!” God set watchmen over them and told them to listen for the ram's horn. They answered that one too. “We will not listen!” Two refusals, plain and final, from a people who still brought their offerings on time.

The offerings are refused in the same sermon. “What use to Me is frankincense from Sheba or sweet cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable; your sacrifices do not please Me.” God is not negotiating for better worship. The army from the north is described one last time, close and unhurried. “They grasp the bow and spear; they are cruel and merciless.” Hands hang limp at the report of it. The city is told to mourn the way a parent mourns an only son, because the destroyer will come suddenly, in the middle of ordinary life.

The sermon closes with Jeremiah given a new job inside the old one: assayer. “I have appointed you to examine My people like ore, so you may know and try their ways.” The picture is a furnace and a man working it for nothing. The people are bronze and iron, every one of them corrupt. “The bellows blow fiercely, blasting away the lead with fire. The refining proceeds in vain, for the wicked are not purged.” The fire is real, the work is real, and the metal will not separate. So the assayer writes the verdict on the batch, and the verdict is the sermon's title and the city's new name. “They are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them.”

title: The Temple Sermon
subtitle: Jeremiah 7
description: Standing in the gate of the LORD's house, Jeremiah tells the worshipers not to trust in the temple chant, and the sermon nearly ends him.
paragraphs: God sends Jeremiah to stand in the gate of the house of the LORD, where everyone entering to worship has to pass him, and the sermon he preaches there is aimed at the building behind him. It begins with a real offer. “Correct your ways and deeds, and I will let you live in this place.” Then it names the slogan the offer has to break through. The worshipers have a chant, and they trust it the way people trust a charm. “This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.” God's answer is that the chant is a deceptive word, and He replaces it with conditions that have nothing to do with the building: act justly toward one another, stop oppressing the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow, stop shedding innocent blood, stop following other gods.

The sermon then reads the worshipers their own week. “Will you steal and murder, commit adultery and perjury, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods that you have not known, and then come and stand before Me in this house, which bears My Name”? And their defense, as God quotes it back to them, is that the house itself has acquitted them. “We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations.” It is the whole theology of the place in one sentence: the temple as a pardon that renews itself every visit, no matter what the visitor goes back to. God's reply turns their sacred word into an accusation. “Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?” A den is not where robbers do their robbing. It is where they go to be safe afterward.

Then God gives them homework in geography. Go to Shiloh, He says, the place where He first made a dwelling for His name, and look at what stands there now: nothing, because of the wickedness of His people Israel. A ruined shrine is God's chosen illustration for a sermon about an unruinable temple. “Therefore what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust.” And folded into the sermon is the hardest instruction Jeremiah has received so far, harder than the preaching itself. “As for you, do not pray for these people, do not offer a plea or petition on their behalf, and do not beg Me, for I will not listen to you.” The prophet's instinct is to intercede. God forbids the instinct.

Outside the gate, the religion of the home goes on undisturbed, and God describes it as a family project. The sons gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven. It is not rebellion in a dark corner. It is the whole household at work together. Against it, God reaches back to the Exodus and states what He actually asked for at the start. The command was not first about burnt offerings and sacrifices. It was this: “Obey Me, and I will be your God, and you will be My people.” From that day to Jeremiah's, the record runs the other way. “They went backward and not forward.” And the sermon's summary of the nation is four words long. “Truth has perished; it has disappeared from their lips.”

The sermon ends where the city's worship and its cruelty meet. In the Valley of Ben-hinnom they have built the high places of Topheth to burn their sons and daughters in the fire, and God disowns the idea in the strongest terms available to Him. It was “something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind.” The valley will be renamed for its future. It will be called “the Valley of Slaughter,” and they will bury the dead in Topheth until there is no more room. And the temple city that rang with festival noise will hear its signature sound removed. “I will remove from the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem the sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of the bride and bridegroom, for the land will become a wasteland.” Hold on to that sound, the bridegroom's voice in the streets. This book will bring it back, but not soon, and not cheaply.

title: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
subtitle: Jeremiah 8
description: The daughter of God's people is wounded, there is no balm and no physician, and the harvest passes with no rescue.
paragraphs: The judgment in this sermon reaches past the living and into the graveyards. When the invasion is done, the tombs of Jerusalem will be opened and the bones brought out: the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of the officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the people. They will be spread in the open before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, the powers these people loved and served and consulted and worshiped. No one will gather them for burial. “Their bones will not be gathered up or buried, but will become like dung lying on the ground.” And for the remnant scattered by the invasion, God gives a sentence that measures the depth of the ruin. “And wherever I have banished them, the remnant of this evil family will choose death over life.”

Then the sermon argues with the people about the simplest motion in the world. Men fall and get up again. A man turns away from a road and turns back. Why does Jerusalem only ever turn away? “They cling to deceit; they refuse to return.” God has listened carefully to the city's talk, He says, and nobody in it repents and asks what he has done. Every man runs his own course “like a horse charging into battle,” head down, full speed, no steering. It is not that return is hard. It is that return has stopped occurring to anyone.

Against that, Jeremiah sets a bird. “Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons. The turtledove, the swift, and the thrush keep their time of migration, but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD.” The stork has no law, no prophet, no temple, and it knows when to go and when to come back. God's people have all three and do not know. Their experts cover the ignorance with credentials. They say, “We are wise, and the Law of the LORD is with us.” God answers that the document itself has been doctored in the handling: “the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception.” And over the whole sickness the official treatment continues, the same words as before, the wound of the daughter of God's people dressed with very little care and a cry of peace, peace, where there is no peace.

The invasion is by now so close that its sounds arrive ahead of it, the snorting of horses heard from Dan, the whole land quaking at the neighing. God adds a quieter weapon of His own. “For behold, I will send snakes among you, vipers that cannot be charmed, and they will bite you.” And then the sermon does something strange: it lets the people speak from the far side of the disaster, as if the exile were already present and Jeremiah could hear it coming. Their voice rises from a land far away. “Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?” And their summary of everything the prophets had promised them is one sentence of pure desolation. “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.”

Jeremiah answers that voice not with an argument but with a wound of his own. “For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed. I mourn; horror has gripped me.” His sorrow, he says, is beyond healing, and his heart is faint within him. Then he asks the question this sermon is remembered by, and the chapter ends without God answering it. Gilead, across the Jordan, was famous for its healing balm and its physicians. “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?” The medicine exists. The doctors exist. The patient is not recovering. The question is left standing in the air, and it will take the rest of the book to answer it.

title: A Fountain of Tears
subtitle: Jeremiah 9
description: Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain, for a people whose tongues bend like bows to shoot lies.
paragraphs: This sermon belongs to Jeremiah before it belongs to the people, and it opens with the prophet wishing his body were built for grief. “Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people.” His second wish follows immediately, and it pulls the opposite direction. If only he had a traveler's lodge in the wilderness, he would abandon his people and depart from them. Weeping over them forever and leaving them forever sit in the same breath, and Jeremiah never resolves the two. The book will show him living both wishes at once for forty years.

What he would be leaving is a society where speech itself has been weaponized. “They bend their tongues like bows; lies prevail over truth in the land.” God warns every man in it to guard against his own neighbor. “Let everyone guard against his neighbor; do not trust any brother, for every brother deals craftily, and every friend spreads slander.” The lying is not a lapse. It is a trained skill. “Each one betrays his friend; no one tells the truth. They have taught their tongues to lie.” And God locates Himself inside the damage: “You dwell in the midst of deception; in their deceit they refuse to know Me.”

God's response to a people like this is the furnace again, the assayer's work from the earlier sermon, but now He explains why He keeps at it. “Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do because of the daughter of My people?” The refining is almost a confession of limited options, as if judgment were the last tool left in the box. The evidence for it is the double life of every mouth in the city. “With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.” Jeremiah takes up the weeping himself, over the land this time. “I will take up a weeping and wailing for the mountains, a dirge over the wilderness pasture,” where the cattle are gone and the birds have fled. And the city's sentence is stated without decoration. “I will make Jerusalem a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals.”

Then God calls for professionals. Grief this large needs people trained to carry it. “Take note, and summon the wailing women; send for the most skillful among them.” They are to teach their daughters to wail and their neighbors to lament, because the disaster has a new address now. “For death has climbed in through our windows; it has entered our fortresses to cut off the children from the streets, the young men from the town squares.” Death is pictured inside the houses, past the defenses, taking the young in the places where the young gather. Zion's own wailing is heard in the sermon before it happens: “How devastated we are! How great is our shame! For we have abandoned the land because our dwellings have been torn down.”

Out of the lament, God sets down the standard by which every boast in the nation will be measured. “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches.” Wisdom, power, and money are the three currencies the city trusts, and all three are dismissed in a single verse. “But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth.” That is the one boast God honors, and He says why: “for I delight in these things.” The sermon ends with the mark of the covenant itself. The days are coming when God will punish all who are circumcised only in the flesh, and the list of the punished runs Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah's name set down among the nations without distinction. “The whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.” The sign they carry in the body has never reached the place it was meant to mark.

title: Scarecrows in a Cucumber Patch
subtitle: Jeremiah 10
description: The idols of the nations are scarecrows in a cucumber patch, set against the God who made the earth by His power.
paragraphs: This sermon is a tour of a workshop. God tells His people not to learn the ways of the nations or tremble at signs in the heavens, and then He walks them through how a god gets made. “For the customs of the peoples are worthless; they cut down a tree from the forest; it is shaped with a chisel by the hands of a craftsman.” “They adorn it with silver and gold and fasten it with hammer and nails, so that it will not totter.” The finished product is installed in the sermon under an image nobody in Judah would forget. “Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch, their idols cannot speak. They must be carried because they cannot walk.” A scarecrow is built to frighten birds and fools nobody who gets close. And the verdict on every god in the workshop is total in both directions: “for they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good.”

Against the workshop the sermon sets a confession. “There is none like You, O LORD. You are great, and Your name is mighty in power.” The nations' wise men and kingdoms are searched, and no rival is found. “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King. The earth quakes at His wrath, and the nations cannot endure His indignation.” One verse of the sermon stands in Aramaic in the text, the language of the empire now rising in the north, as if the message were already addressed to the world the exiles would live in. “These gods, who have made neither the heavens nor the earth, will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.” Gods that made nothing will outlast nothing.

The shame lands on the makers, not just the made. “Every man is senseless and devoid of knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols. For his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them.” Israel's God is defined against all of it by a name this sermon gives Him. “The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things, and Israel is the tribe of His inheritance.” Other nations inherit gods. Jacob's inheritance is God Himself. And then the sermon turns from the workshop to the street, and the warning is practical and immediate. “Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege.”

The reason is God's own image for the exile, and it is not a march or a caravan. “Behold, at this time I will sling out the inhabitants of the land and bring distress upon them so that they may be captured.” A stone in a sling does not choose its direction. The city answers in the sermon in her own voice, already wounded. “Woe to me because of my brokenness; my wound is grievous!” Her tent is destroyed, its ropes snapped, her sons departed, and no one left to pitch it again. The blame is placed where this book always places it. “For the shepherds have become senseless; they do not seek the LORD. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered.” From the north, the report is already audible.

The sermon ends with Jeremiah praying for himself, and the prayer is more honest than comfortable. “I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps.” The prophet who has just announced that lives are slung out of the land asks to be handled differently from the nations. “Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice,” he prays, and not in anger, because anger from God would reduce him to nothing. The wrath he will not ask for himself he asks onto the nations that devoured Jacob. “Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, and on the families that do not call on Your name.” Jeremiah knows exactly which side of the judgment he stands on. He is asking to be corrected, not consumed, and the distinction will matter for the rest of his life.

title: The Covenant and the Plot
subtitle: Jeremiah 11
description: Jeremiah proclaims the broken covenant through Judah, and his own town of Anathoth plots to kill him for it.
paragraphs: God sends Jeremiah back to the founding document. The word of this chapter is the covenant itself, the one made when God brought the fathers out of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, and the sermon reads its terms aloud in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. The terms open with the curse clause. “Cursed is the man who does not obey the words of this covenant.” The condition from the beginning had been obedience, and the land flowing with milk and honey was the oath built on it. Jeremiah answers the reading the way the people were supposed to answer it, and his answer carries the whole tragedy of the chapter in one breath: Amen, LORD.

Then God states the charge in a word Jeremiah has not used before. “There is a conspiracy among the men of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem.” Not a drift, not a weakness. A conspiracy: the nation has returned to the sins of the forefathers on purpose, in concert, and broken the covenant from both houses at once. The outcome is stated just as plainly. “I am about to bring upon them a disaster that they cannot escape. They will cry out to Me, but I will not listen to them.” They will cry to their other gods too, and the sermon has already counted those. “Your gods are indeed as numerous as your cities, O Judah.” And for the second time in three chapters, God closes the prophet's own mouth as an intercessor. “As for you, do not pray for these people. Do not raise up a cry or a prayer on their behalf, for I will not be listening when they call out to Me in their time of disaster.”

The image God reaches for is one He planted Himself. “The LORD once called you a flourishing olive tree, beautiful with well-formed fruit. But with a mighty roar He will set it on fire, and its branches will be consumed.” The LORD of Hosts, who planted the tree, has decreed the fire. That is where the chapter turns, because the next thing Jeremiah learns is not about the nation at all. It is about the men sharpening knives for the preacher. “And the LORD informed me, so I knew. Then You showed me their deeds.”

Jeremiah had been preaching in his hometown's reach without knowing what his hometown was saying about him. “For I was like a gentle lamb led to slaughter; I did not know that they had plotted against me.” The plotters' words are recorded in full, and they are arborists' words, aimed at a tree and its fruit. “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit; let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be remembered no more.” They do not only want him dead. They want the name gone, the memory erased, the sermon and the serman's household with it. Jeremiah's response is the first of his great prayers of appeal, and it does not ask for escape. “O LORD of Hosts, who judges righteously, who examines the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause.” He hands the case upward and keeps preaching.

God names the plotters for him: the people of Anathoth, his own town, the priestly town he grew up in. Their ultimatum is quoted as evidence. “You must not prophesy in the name of the LORD, or you will die by our hand.” The men who inherited the priesthood are threatening the prophet for prophesying, in the name of the LORD they serve. The sentence God pronounces is total and dated. Their young men will die by the sword, their sons and daughters by famine. “There will be no remnant, for I will bring disaster on the people of Anathoth in the year of their punishment.” Jeremiah will go on preaching. But from this chapter on, he preaches as a man who knows the first death threat against him came from home.

title: Why Do the Wicked Prosper?
subtitle: Jeremiah 12
description: Jeremiah pleads his righteous case and asks why the treacherous thrive; the answer sends him from a footrace to horses.
paragraphs: The plot at Anathoth sends Jeremiah to God with a lawsuit of his own, and he opens it like a man who knows the verdict before he argues the case. “Righteous are You, O LORD, when I plead before You. Yet about Your judgments I wish to contend with You: Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all the faithless live at ease?” The men who just threatened to kill him are not struggling. They are thriving, and Jeremiah says the thriving is God's own doing. “You planted them, and they have taken root. They have grown and produced fruit. You are ever on their lips, but far from their hearts.” Their religion talks about God constantly and keeps Him nowhere near the center. The prophet, meanwhile, stands in the open. “But You know me, O LORD; You see me and test my heart toward You.”

His complaint is not only personal. The land itself is suffering under the arrangement. “How long will the land mourn and the grass of every field be withered?” The animals and birds have been swept away because of the evil of the residents, and the residents are untroubled by it, because they have decided the prophet cannot be right about the future. “He cannot see what our end will be.” That sentence is the real target of the chapter. Jeremiah can bear being threatened. What he cannot bear is a world where threatening him works, where evil is planted and watered and harvested while the man who tells the truth is marked for erasure.

God's answer is the hardest word Jeremiah has received, and it is not an answer to the question. God never explains why the wicked prosper. Instead He measures Jeremiah's suffering and calls it the easy part. “If you have raced with men on foot and they have worn you out, how can you compete with horses? If you stumble in a peaceful land, how will you do in the thickets of the Jordan?” Anathoth was men on foot. Jerusalem will be horses. And God adds the detail that makes the footrace what it was: it was not strangers. His own father's household has betrayed him and cried aloud against him. “Do not trust them, though they speak well of you.” The prophet is being trained by betrayal, and the training is deliberate, and it is not finished.

Then the chapter does something unexpected. God takes up the grief Himself, and His grief is larger than the prophet's. “I have forsaken My house; I have abandoned My inheritance. I have given the beloved of My soul into the hands of her enemies.” The beloved of His soul: that is what He calls the people He is handing over. His inheritance has become a lion roaring at Him in the forest, a speckled bird circled by birds of prey. “Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard; they have trampled My plot of ground. They have turned My pleasant field into a desolate wasteland.” The destroyers range over the whole land, and the summary is absolute: “the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other. No flesh has peace.” The farmer's version of the same ruin follows. “They have sown wheat but harvested thorns. They have exhausted themselves to no avail.”

The chapter ends with the nations around Judah, the evil neighbors who helped themselves to Israel's inheritance, and God's handling of them widens in a way this book has not shown before. They will be uprooted from their land, and Judah uprooted from among them. “But after I have uprooted them, I will once again have compassion on them and return each one to his inheritance and to his land.” More than that: if those nations learn the ways of God's people and learn to swear the oath Israel was always meant to swear, “As surely as the LORD lives,” then they will be established among His people. The confession that began with one prophet asking why the wicked prosper ends with the wicked nations offered a place inside the people of God, if they will learn His ways. Jeremiah asked about his plotters. God answered with the whole map.

title: The Ruined Loincloth
subtitle: Jeremiah 13
description: A new loincloth buried by the Euphrates comes back ruined, and the pride of Judah is read aloud from its rot.
paragraphs: The next sermon Jeremiah preaches is one he has to wear. God sends him to buy a linen loincloth and put it on, with a strange instruction: do not let it touch water. So Jeremiah buys the cloth and wears it unwashed, close against his body, as the word of the LORD directed. Then the word comes a second time. Take the loincloth he is wearing and go at once to Perath and hide it in a crevice of the rocks. Jeremiah goes and hides it there. Many days later the word comes again. Go back to Perath and get the loincloth. He digs it out of the rocks, and the sermon is standing there in his hands: ruined, rotted through, of no use at all.

God interprets His own object lesson in one sentence. “In the same way I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem.” The evil people who refuse to listen, who follow the stubbornness of their own hearts and go after other gods, “they will be like this loincloth.” Then God tells Jeremiah what the cloth had been for, and the purpose is tender enough to make the ruin hurt. “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s waist, so I have made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to Me, declares the LORD, so that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory. But they did not listen.” Closeness was the design. The people of God were made to be worn against Him, for His renown and praise and glory. The distance they chose is the rot.

The chapter carries a second sign, this one spoken in the street like a riddle. The saying goes that every wineskin shall be filled with wine, and when Jeremiah delivers it, the people answer with the obvious: don't we know that? Then the word turns on them. “I am going to fill with drunkenness all who live in this land,” the kings and priests and prophets and everyone in Jerusalem, “I will smash them against one another, fathers and sons alike, declares the LORD. I will allow no mercy or pity or compassion to keep Me from destroying them.” The filled wineskins are people, and what fills them is not celebration. It is a staggering that ends with a nation smashing itself apart.

The warning that follows is timed to the last of the light. “Give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the dusky mountains.” And Jeremiah confesses what the preaching costs him where no audience can see it. “But if you do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your pride. My eyes will overflow with tears, because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.” The secret weeping is over pride, the same pride the ruined cloth named. Then the sermon addresses the throne itself. Say to the king and to the queen mother: “Take a lowly seat, for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads.” The cities of the Negev are already shut tight in the vision, and all Judah carried into exile.

When the people ask the question the whole book keeps hearing, why has this happened to me, the answer is the magnitude of their iniquity. And then God states the depth of the habit in an image that has stayed famous ever since. “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” A people accustomed to doing evil, God says, is no more able to do good than a leopard is able to rearrange its own coat. The lot is measured out and delivered. “This is your lot, the portion I have measured to you,” and the charge under it is not idolatry this time but forgetfulness: “because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood.” The chapter ends with the city addressed by name and left with a question instead of a sentence. “Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will you remain unclean?”

title: Drought, and Do Not Pray
subtitle: Jeremiah 14
description: The land mourns without water, the prophets lie about peace, and God tells Jeremiah not to pray for this people.
paragraphs: This word came to Jeremiah concerning the drought, and the drought is described before anyone prays about it. Judah mourns and her gates languish. The nobles send their servants to the cisterns and the servants come back with empty jars, ashamed, covering their heads. “The ground is cracked because no rain has fallen on the land.” The farmers cover their heads too. The failure reaches the animals, who have no sins to confess: “Even the doe in the field deserts her newborn fawn because there is no grass.” Wild donkeys stand on the barren heights panting like jackals, their eyes going dim for lack of pasture. The broken cisterns of the early sermons are now literal, and they are empty.

Out of the drought the people produce a prayer, and it is a good prayer. It confesses before it asks. “Although our iniquities testify against us, O LORD, act for the sake of Your name. Indeed, our rebellions are many; we have sinned against You.” It appeals to who God is: “O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress, why are You like a stranger in the land, like a traveler who stays but a night?” It presses the relationship. “Yet You are among us, O LORD, and we are called by Your name. Do not forsake us!” Confession, God's name, God's presence, God's covenant people: everything Jeremiah's sermons have demanded is in it. And God refuses it.

The refusal explains itself, and the explanation is a habit, not a moment. “Truly they love to wander; they have not restrained their feet. So the LORD does not accept them; He will now remember their iniquity and punish them for their sins.” Then, for the third time in the book, the instruction lands on Jeremiah personally. “Do not pray for the well-being of this people.” Fasting will not open the door. “Although they may fast, I will not listen to their cry; although they may offer burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them. Instead, I will finish them off by sword and famine and plague.” The prayer was good. It was also late, and it came from people who loved to wander and intended to keep wandering.

Jeremiah tries once more, and his defense of the people is that they have been misled. Look, he says, the prophets are telling them the opposite of disaster. Their promise stands in the text as the drought deepens around it: “You will not see the sword or suffer famine, but I will give you lasting peace in this place.” God's answer separates the shepherds from the sheep only to judge both. “The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,” He says. “I did not send them or appoint them or speak to them.” They prophesy a false vision, the delusion of their own minds, and their sentence is the disaster they denied. “By sword and famine these very prophets will meet their end!” The people who believed them will be thrown into the streets unburied, wives and sons and daughters with them. God calls it pouring out their own evil upon them.

What Jeremiah is given instead of an answered prayer is a word of tears to speak aloud, his own grief assigned as the message. “My eyes overflow with tears; day and night they do not cease, for the virgin daughter of my people has been shattered by a crushing blow, a severely grievous wound.” Inside the city, famine; outside it, the sword: “If I go out to the country, I see those slain by the sword; if I enter the city, I see those ravaged by famine!” And still the chapter ends with the people praying again, and praying better. “We acknowledge our wickedness, O LORD, the guilt of our fathers; indeed, we have sinned against You.” Their last argument is weather. “Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? Is this not by You, O LORD our God? So we put our hope in You, for You have done all these things.” It is the right prayer, to the right God, for the right reason. The chapter closes on it, and heaven does not answer in the chapter.

title: Even Moses and Samuel
subtitle: Jeremiah 15
description: Not even Moses and Samuel could turn God now, and Jeremiah's own complaint is answered with a call to return himself.
paragraphs: God opens this chapter by naming the two greatest intercessors in Israel's history and retiring them both. “Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people. Send them from My presence, and let them go!” Moses had stood in the breach after the golden calf and turned God's wrath away. Samuel had prayed a nation back from its panic. Neither name carries weight anymore, not because the men have diminished but because the case is closed. If the people ask where they are supposed to go, Jeremiah is to read them their destinations: to death, to the sword, to famine, to captivity. “I will appoint over them four kinds of destroyers, declares the LORD: the sword to kill, the dogs to drag away, and the birds of the air and beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.”

The stated cause reaches back two generations. God will make Judah a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth “because of what Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah did in Jerusalem.” Manasseh is dead. His grandson Josiah's reforms are also past. The judgment still carries Manasseh's name, a reminder that in this book a king's evil can outlive everyone who committed it. Over the city God pronounces a weariness that sounds almost human. “You have forsaken Me, declares the LORD. You have turned your back. So I will stretch out My hand against you and I will destroy you; I am weary of showing compassion.” Widows will outnumber the sand of the sea. “The mother of seven will grow faint; she will breathe her last breath. Her sun will set while it is still day.”

Then the chapter turns inward, and Jeremiah lodges the complaint that has been building since Anathoth. “Woe to me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife and conflict in all the land. I have neither lent nor borrowed, yet everyone curses me.” He has made no loans and taken none; he has wronged no one in business; and the whole land curses him for the sermons. God answers briefly, a promise inside the refusal: “Surely I will deliver you for a good purpose.” But Jeremiah is not finished, and his prayer sharpens into a request for payback. “You understand, O LORD; remember me and attend to me. Avenge me against my persecutors.”

What he says next is the most loved sentence he ever speaks, and it explains how a man keeps preaching sermons that everyone hates. “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart’s delight. For I bear Your name, O LORD God of Hosts.” The words were food and joy before they were a burden. But bearing the name has cost him every ordinary pleasure. “I never sat with the band of revelers, nor did I celebrate with them. Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone, for You have filled me with indignation.” And then the complaint goes all the way down, past the people, to God Himself. “Why is my pain unending, and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? You have indeed become like a mirage to me,” a stream in the desert that shows water, “water that is not there.” The prophet of the fountain of living water accuses God of being a broken cistern.

God's reply to His own prophet is the same word He has been giving Israel all along: return. “If you return, I will restore you; you will stand in My presence. And if you speak words that are noble instead of worthless, you will be My spokesman.” Jeremiah must separate the noble from the worthless in his own speech, the complaint from the calling, and let the people turn to him rather than turning to them. And then God renews the promise of the first chapter almost word for word. “Then I will make you a wall to this people, a fortified wall of bronze; they will fight against you but will not overcome you, for I am with you to save and deliver you, declares the LORD.” “I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked and redeem you from the grasp of the ruthless.” The closed case against Judah does not close the case for Jeremiah. He is corrected, recommissioned, and sent back to the same streets.

title: You Must Not Marry
subtitle: Jeremiah 16
description: Jeremiah is forbidden a wife, a funeral, and a feast in that place, three empty rooms preaching the withdrawal of peace.
paragraphs: The next sermon is not preached. It is lived. God forbids Jeremiah the three rooms where ordinary life happens. First, the wedding: “You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place.” The reason is the fate of the children being born in Judah now. “They will die from deadly diseases. They will not be mourned or buried, but will lie like dung on the ground.” They will be finished off by sword and famine, and their bodies will feed the birds and the beasts. A prophet with no family is not a private arrangement in this book. It is a public sign, walking the streets for years: here is a man with no future in this land, because this land has no future for children.

Second, the funeral. “Do not enter a house where there is a funeral meal. Do not go to mourn or show sympathy, for I have removed from this people My peace, My loving devotion, and My compassion.” Jeremiah is barred from the mourning customs of his own people, the food offered to comfort the bereaved, the cup of consolation for a father's or a mother's death, at the exact time when mourning is about to become the national occupation. Great and small will die unburied and unmourned, and the prophet will not be permitted to soften one funeral. Third, the feast. He must not enter a house of celebration and sit down to eat and drink, because God is removing the soundtrack of ordinary joy: “I am going to remove from this place, before your very eyes and in your days, the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom.” It is the sentence from the temple sermon, now with a witness assigned: Jeremiah will hear the silence happen.

When the people hear all this, God predicts their question, and it is the question of people who genuinely do not connect their lives with their disaster. “Why has the LORD pronounced all this great disaster against us? What is our iniquity? What is the sin that we have committed against the LORD our God?” The answer reaches back before they were born and then lands on them. Their fathers forsook God, followed other gods, served and worshiped them, abandoned Him and broke His instruction. “And you have done more evil than your fathers.” Each man follows the stubbornness of his own evil heart instead of obeying. “So I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known. There you will serve other gods day and night, for I will show you no favor.” In exile they will finally get what they always wanted, gods in abundance, and no favor with them.

Then, inside the chapter of the bans, the book makes one of its sudden turns toward a future bigger than the judgment. A day is coming when Israel's founding story will be retold with a new Exodus at its center. They will no longer swear by the LORD “who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.” They will swear by the LORD “who brought the Israelites up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.” The return will outshine the Exodus itself. But the road there runs through the hunt. “But for now I will send for many fishermen, declares the LORD, and they will catch them. After that I will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them down on every mountain and hill, even from the clefts of the rocks.” God's eyes are on all their ways. First the double repayment for defiling His land. Then the gathering, and the gathering begins as a manhunt.

Jeremiah answers the chapter with a prayer that looks past Judah entirely. “O LORD, my strength and my fortress, my refuge in the day of distress,” he prays, and then he sees the nations coming to God from the ends of the earth with a confession of their own: “Our fathers inherited nothing but lies, worthless idols of no benefit at all.” The fraud will be confessed by the defrauded. “Can man make gods for himself? Such are not gods!” And God's final word in the chapter takes that confession and makes it the lesson plan for the world. This time He will teach them His power and His might, “then they will know that My name is the LORD.”

title: The Tree Planted by the Waters
subtitle: Jeremiah 17
description: A shrub in the desert and a tree by the waters are set side by side, and the Sabbath is preached at the gates of the city.
paragraphs: The chapter opens with a writing instrument. Judah's sin, God says, is not penciled onto the people, where weather could fade it. “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars.” Diamond cuts what iron cannot scratch. The sin is engraved in the two places that define the nation, the heart inside and the altar outside, and the children grow up remembering the Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills the way other children remember their fathers' houses. For this, the inheritance God gave them will be handed over as plunder, and they will serve their enemies in a land they do not know.

Then the sermon sets two plantings side by side, and they are the two futures available to every person hearing it. “Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes mere flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD.” “He will be like a shrub in the desert; he will not see when prosperity comes.” He lives in parched places, in a salt land where no one lives, and his tragedy is not only thirst. Good passes by and he cannot even see it. “But blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose confidence is in Him.” “He is like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream. It does not fear when the heat comes, and its leaves are always green. It does not worry in a year of drought, nor does it cease to produce fruit.” A year of drought: Jeremiah has just preached through one, in a land of cracked ground and empty cisterns. The tree of this sermon has its roots down to water that drought cannot reach, and it keeps producing fruit in the very conditions that kill the shrub.

Between the plantings stands the reason the choice is so hard to see from inside. “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?” The engraved heart of the first verse and the deceitful heart of this one are the same organ. It cannot audit itself. “I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way, by what his deeds deserve.” Wealth gathered crookedly gets a farm image of its own, a partridge sitting on eggs it did not lay, warming a fortune that will desert its owner mid-life and leave him the fool at the end. And above all of it the chapter sets the address of real safety: the glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, the place of the sanctuary. “O LORD, the hope of Israel,” the sermon names Him, and returns to the fountain of the early chapters when it describes those who leave: “they have abandoned the LORD, the fountain of living water.”

Jeremiah's own prayer grows out of that ground. “Heal me, O LORD, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, for You are my praise.” Around him the mockery has become a refrain of its own, and the people chant it at the prophet whose predictions keep not happening on their schedule: “Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!” Jeremiah answers the charge by testifying to his own reluctance. “But I have not run away from being Your shepherd; I have not desired the day of despair.” He did not want this message. He asks God not to become a terror to him, since God is his refuge in the day of disaster, and then the prayer hardens toward his persecutors in the pattern of the confessions: “Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame.”

The chapter ends with a sermon at the gates about carrying. God stations Jeremiah at the gate of the people, where the kings of Judah pass in and out, and at every other gate of Jerusalem, to preach the Sabbath: carry no load through the gates on the Sabbath day, bring nothing out of your houses, do no work, keep the day holy as the fathers were commanded. Their fathers stiffened their necks at exactly this. Now the condition is set out with the whole future of the city hanging on a day of rest. If they listen, “then kings and princes will enter through the gates of this city. They will sit on the throne of David,” riding in chariots and on horses, “and this city will be inhabited forever.” If they do not, God will kindle “an unquenchable fire in its gates to consume the citadels of Jerusalem.” A sermon about not carrying loads becomes a referendum on whether David's throne stands. The gates where the loads come in are the gates Jeremiah is watching.

title: The Potter's House
subtitle: Jeremiah 18
description: At the potter's wheel a spoiled vessel is remade, and Judah answers the offer with a shrug: that is in vain.
paragraphs: God sends Jeremiah down to the potter's house for this sermon, and the lesson is already in motion when he arrives. The potter is working at the wheel, shaping a vessel from the clay, and while Jeremiah watches, the vessel becomes flawed in the potter's hand. The potter does not throw it away. He forms it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do. Only then does the word come. “O house of Israel, declares the LORD, can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay? Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel.”

What follows is the operating principle behind every sermon in this book, stated by God as policy. When He announces that a nation will be uprooted, torn down, and destroyed, the announcement is not a lock. “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring.” The rule runs in the other direction too: a nation God announces He will build up and establish can do evil, refuse His voice, and forfeit the good He intended. God's spoken plans are real, and they are responsive. The clay can still be reworked. That is why the potter sermon ends as an appeal rather than a sentence. “Behold, I am planning a disaster for you and devising a plan against you. Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.”

And the people answer the appeal in advance, in God's own quotation of them, and the answer is the most self-aware sentence in the book so far. “It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.” They call their own hearts stubborn and evil and choose them anyway. Nature itself is more faithful. “Does the snow of Lebanon ever leave its rocky slopes? Or do its cool waters flowing from a distance ever run dry?” The snow stays. The streams flow. “Yet My people have forgotten Me.” They have left the ancient roads for rutted bypaths, and the God they forgot announces what a forgotten God looks like in the day of calamity: “I will scatter them before the enemy like the east wind. I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.”

The sermon produces a plot, and the plotters' reasoning shows how secure the religious establishment feels. “Come, let us make plans against Jeremiah, for the law will never be lost to the priest, nor counsel to the wise, nor an oracle to the prophet. Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” Their confidence is institutional: priests, wise men, and prophets are permanent fixtures, so one troublesome prophet is replaceable, and his words can simply be ignored as a body. Jeremiah's existence threatens nothing structural, in their accounting. They can denounce him and the system will go on without a tremor.

Jeremiah's prayer answers the plot by entering his own record into evidence. “Attend to me, O LORD. Hear what my accusers are saying!” “Should good be repaid with evil? Yet they have dug a pit for me. Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them.” This is the prayer God three times forbade him to pray, and Jeremiah did pray it, standing between the wrath and the people who are now digging his pit. The rest of the prayer asks for their children given to famine, their wives widowed and childless, their young men struck down in battle, and it ends with a refusal to forgive on God's behalf: “But You, O LORD, know all their deadly plots against me. Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight.” The book does not clean this prayer up. The man who ate God's words and called them his joy also prayed this, and both prayers stand in the record side by side.

title: The Smashed Jar
subtitle: Jeremiah 19:1-20:6
description: A flask is smashed in the valley and a priest is renamed Terror on Every Side, in the sermon that runs from Topheth to the stocks.
paragraphs: The potter appears again, but this time Jeremiah is not sent to watch. He is sent to buy. God tells him to purchase a clay jar and take some of the elders of the people and the leaders of the priests out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, by the entrance of the Potsherd Gate, the gate where broken pottery was thrown away. The audience is the city's senior leadership, and the location is its place of child sacrifice. The charge is read to them standing in it. God is bringing such disaster on this place “that the ears of all who hear of it will ring,” because they abandoned Him there and filled the valley with other gods. “They have filled this place with the blood of the innocent.”

The center of the charge is Topheth. “They have built high places to Baal on which to burn their children in the fire as offerings to Baal.” And God disowns the practice with the same sentence He used in the temple sermon, expanded by one word. It was “something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind.” The valley's name will not survive its crimes. The days are coming “when this place will no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter,” a burial ground that will fill until there is no more room. The city's own plans will be ruined in the place where she ruined her children, her corpses given to the birds and beasts, and the siege will drive her to the valley's own horror at home: “I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and they will eat one another’s flesh in the siege and distress inflicted on them by their enemies who seek their lives.”

Then Jeremiah does what he was brought there to do. In the presence of the elders and priests, he shatters the jar. “I will shatter this nation and this city, like one shatters a potter’s jar that can never again be repaired.” The two potter sermons stand back to back and must be read together. At the wheel, the clay was wet and flawed and the potter formed it into another vessel; the nation was offered exactly that. A fired jar is past the wheel. What is shattered now cannot be re-formed, only buried, and the burial place is Topheth itself. “I will make this city like Topheth.” Jeremiah then walks back up to the temple and stands in its courtyard and delivers the valley sermon to all the people: “Behold, I am about to bring on this city and on all the villages around it every disaster I have pronounced against them, because they have stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words.”

The courtyard sermon gets him arrested. Pashhur the priest, son of Immer, the chief official in the house of the LORD, has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, by the temple, where the whole city can see the prophet displayed. He stays there through the night. The next day Pashhur lets him out, and the man who comes out of the stocks gives the official a new name. “The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but Magor-missabib.” The name means terror on every side.

The sentence attached to the name is the invasion, personalized. “I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies before your very eyes.” The wealth of the city and the treasures of its kings will be carried to Babylon, and the chief official will go with them. “And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity. You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried,” Jeremiah says, “you and all your friends to whom you have prophesied these lies.” Pashhur had a counter-sermon, of peace and safety, and the stocks were his argument for it. The name Jeremiah gives him will outlast the argument. Terror on every side is about to become the most quoted phrase in the prophet's life, and not by him.

title: Fire in My Bones
subtitle: Jeremiah 20:7-18
description: Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him, cannot hold the fire in, sings one verse, and curses the day he was born.
paragraphs: Out of the stocks, Jeremiah turns on the One who sent him, and the prayer he prays is the most dangerous of his confessions. “You have deceived me, O LORD, and I was deceived. You have overcome me and prevailed. I am a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me.” God had promised at his call that his opponents would never overcome him. Jeremiah's experience runs the other way: he is overcome, and by God. The content of the preaching is the problem. “For whenever I speak, I cry out; I proclaim violence and destruction. For the word of the LORD has become to me a reproach and derision all day long.” He has two words to say in public, violence and destruction, and the city has made him a byword for both.

So he tries to resign, and the resignation fails inside his own body. When he resolves not to mention God or speak any more in His name, the message does not go quiet. “His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail.” Silence costs more than speech. Around him, the whisperers have taken up the name he gave Pashhur and turned it into a taunt with his name inside it: “Terror is on every side! Report him; let us report him!” Even his trusted friends watch for him to stumble, and their hope is quoted without flinching: “Perhaps he will be deceived so that we may prevail against him and take our vengeance upon him.” The deceived prophet is surrounded by people waiting to prove the deception.

Then, in the same prayer, with nothing changed in his circumstances, the confession swings. “But the LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior. Therefore, my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail.” They will be utterly put to shame, “with an everlasting disgrace that will never be forgotten.” Jeremiah re-files his case with the judge he has used since Anathoth: “O LORD of Hosts, who examines the righteous, who sees the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause.” And the prayer reaches all the way to praise, the full-throated kind, in the mouth of a man who was beaten yesterday: “Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD! For He rescues the life of the needy from the hands of evildoers.”

And then, three verses later, the same mouth curses the day he was born. “Cursed be the day I was born! May the day my mother bore me never be blessed.” The curse takes in the messenger who carried the birth announcement to his father, wishing him like the cities God overthrew without compassion, wishing the man had killed the child before the announcement was needed, “because he did not kill me in the womb so that my mother might have been my grave, and her womb forever enlarged.” Nothing in the passage softens it, explains it, or steps between Jeremiah and the words. The praise and the curse stand twelve verses apart in one prayer, and the book records no answer from God to either.

The confession ends as a question with no address left to send it to: “Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, and to end my days in shame?” With this prayer the long sequence of Jeremiah's confessions closes; the book preserves no more of them. What the record shows next is the prophet at work again, answering a king's embassy while the siege is on. The man who could not quit did not quit. The fire stayed in the bones, and the bones kept standing in the gates.

title: The Way of Life and the Way of Death
subtitle: Jeremiah 21
description: With Babylon at the door, Jeremiah sets before the city the way of life and the way of death, and tells the king's messengers God's answer.
paragraphs: The book now steps forward in time. The confessions are behind Jeremiah; King Zedekiah is on the throne, the last king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon is waging war against Jerusalem. The chapters around this one reach back to earlier reigns, but the book places the siege here, at the head of the kings collection, and lets it stand. Zedekiah sends two men to the prophet he has never once obeyed: Pashhur son of Malchijah, a different Pashhur from the official who put Jeremiah in the stocks, and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah. Their errand is a request for a miracle. “Please inquire of the LORD on our behalf, since Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is waging war against us. Perhaps the LORD will perform for us something like all His past wonders, so that Nebuchadnezzar will withdraw from us.”

The answer turns the Exodus upside down. Zedekiah wants the God who once fought for Israel against Egypt. Jeremiah announces the God who will fight against Jerusalem in person. “I will turn against you the weapons of war in your hands, with which you are fighting the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who besiege you outside the wall,” God says, and draw the defenders into the center of the city to face Him. “And I Myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm, with anger, fury, and great wrath.” The outstretched hand and the mighty arm are the signature phrases of the deliverance from Egypt, the words Israel sang about. Here they are aimed at Israel. The real besieger of Jerusalem is not outside the wall. “I will strike down the residents of this city, both man and beast. They will die in a terrible plague.”

What the survivors get from Nebuchadnezzar is stated just as flatly. God will hand Zedekiah, his officers, and the people who outlast plague and sword and famine over to the king of Babylon and to enemies who seek their lives: “He will put them to the sword; he will not spare them or show pity or compassion.” The embassy came asking for a wonder and receives a surrender document. God has set His face against the city to bring disaster and not good, and He will deliver it into Babylon's hand to be destroyed with fire.
