And yet the chapter contains an offer, addressed not to the palace but to the people. “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.” The terms reverse every instinct of loyalty and patriotism. “Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine and plague, but whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans who besiege you will live; he will retain his life like a spoil of war.” Life is outside the walls, through the gate, in the enemy's camp, at the price of being called a traitor. What the surrenderer keeps is named with a phrase this book will use three more times, for an Ethiopian court official, for Jeremiah himself, and for Baruch: his life, retained like spoil carried off a battlefield. In a city under God's own siege, survival itself is the plunder.

The chapter's last word belongs to the palace that sent the embassy, and it is not about Babylon at all. “Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor, or My wrath will go forth like fire and burn with no one to extinguish it because of their evil deeds.” Even now, with the siege on, the word to the house of David is the word it has always been: justice in the morning, the robbed rescued before noon. The kings on their rocky plateau are still saying what their geography taught them: “Who can come against us? Who can enter our dwellings?” God answers that He Himself will kindle a fire in their forest. The embassy got no wonder. It got a diagnosis it had been refusing for twenty years, delivered at the exact moment when refusing it became fatal.

title: Woe to the Kings of the House
subtitle: Jeremiah 22
description: Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah are judged one by one, and a cedar palace is measured against the justice of Josiah.
paragraphs: This chapter is a collection of sermons at the palace, addressed to the kings of Judah one by one, and it opens with the standing terms for all of them. Jeremiah is sent down to the palace to proclaim: “Administer justice and righteousness. Rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor. Do no wrong or violence to the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow. Do not shed innocent blood in this place.” The condition attached is the throne itself. “For if you will indeed carry out these commands, then kings who sit on David’s throne will enter through the gates of this palace riding on chariots and horses.” “But if you do not obey these words, then I swear by Myself, declares the LORD, that this house will become a pile of rubble.” Justice is not one royal virtue among others in this book. It is the lease on the palace.

God describes the palace the way a lover describes what he is about to lose. “You are like Gilead to Me, like the summit of Lebanon; but I will surely turn you into a desert, like cities that are uninhabited.” The destroyers are already appointed, and they will cut down the choicest of its cedars and throw them into the fire, the very timber the kings prized. Afterward, the nations will walk past the ruin and conduct the tour themselves. They will ask one another, “Why has the LORD done such a thing to this great city?” And the answer will be common knowledge: “Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD their God and have worshiped and served other gods.”

The first king addressed is Shallum, called Jehoahaz elsewhere, Josiah's son, who succeeded his father and was taken away. God's instruction about him rearranges the mourning customs: “Do not weep for him who is dead; do not mourn his loss. Weep bitterly for him who is exiled, for he will never return to see his native land.” Josiah, dead in battle, is not the tragedy. The living exile is. Of Shallum, God says, “but he will die in the place to which he was exiled; he will never see this land again.” An exiled king who never comes home is worse off than a dead one, and the chapter will prove the rule again before it ends.

Then comes Jehoiakim, Shallum's brother, and the sermon against him is the angriest in the collection. “Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms without justice, who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages.” Jehoiakim's own boast is quoted against him: “I will build myself a great palace, with spacious upper rooms.” Cedar panels, vermilion paint, unpaid countrymen. God's cross-examination is a single comparison. “Did not your father have food and drink? He administered justice and righteousness, and so it went well with him.” “He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?” Knowing God is defined at the palace as taking up the cause of the poor, and Jehoiakim's file is its opposite: “But your eyes and heart are set on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.” His burial closes the case: “He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.” No mourning refrain, no alas for the master. A donkey's burial for the king of the cedar palace.

The last king is Coniah, Jehoiakim's son, called Jeconiah, and God's image for him is jewelry. “Even if you, Coniah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah, were a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.” A signet ring is the closest, most worn, most identifying object a king owns; God says He would tear it off His own hand. Coniah and his mother will be hurled into a land where neither was born, and there they will both die. “Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?” Then the address swings wide. “O land, land, land, hear the word of the LORD!” And the enrollment that ends the chapter closes the throne question this collection has been circling. “Enroll this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime. None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.” Coniah has sons; the record knows it. Childless here is a legal verdict, not a genealogy: no descendant of his will reign. The Davidic succession, as the kings of Judah have known it, ends in this chapter. What can replace it is the subject of the next one.

title: The LORD Our Righteousness
subtitle: Jeremiah 23
description: False shepherds are sentenced, a righteous Branch is promised, and dreams are weighed as straw against the wheat of the word.
paragraphs: After the kings, the shepherds. “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” In this book the shepherds are the rulers, and the charge is that the flock was not lost but scattered, driven away by the men assigned to attend to it. God's answer begins with a grim play on their job title: “You have scattered My flock and driven them away, and have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds, declares the LORD.” Then the scattering is reversed by the only shepherd left. “Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them, and I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply.” “I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing, declares the LORD.” Not one sheep unaccounted for. It is everything chapter 22's kings were not.

Then the singular. “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land.” Where Coniah was enrolled childless and his line struck from the throne, a Branch from David is promised who does the two things the palace sermons demanded: justice and righteousness, administered by a king who reigns wisely. “In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.” The days of this king carry the new Exodus oath with them, the oath Jeremiah first heard during the marriage bans: no longer the LORD who brought Israel up out of Egypt, but the LORD who brought them up out of the land of the north and all the lands of their banishment, home to dwell in their own land.

The chapter's second half turns from the shepherds to the prophets, and it opens in Jeremiah's body. “My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble. I have become like a drunkard, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD, because of His holy words.” What breaks him is the class he belongs to. “For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness.” Samaria's prophets prophesied by Baal, bad enough. Jerusalem's are worse: “And among the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: They commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns his back on wickedness.” Because the prophets validate the wicked instead of turning them, ungodliness spreads from Jerusalem through the whole land. Their diet is set by God Himself: “I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has spread throughout the land.”

The test God applies to them is a council He keeps. “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.” Their message to everyone who despises God is peace, and to everyone walking in stubbornness, no harm will come. But, God asks, “which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word?” “But if they had stood in My council, they would have proclaimed My words to My people and turned them back from their evil ways and deeds.” A true prophet's sermon turns people. Theirs only soothes. What they traffic in is dreams, and they run through the city crying, “I had a dream! I had a dream!” God's ruling on dreams is not a ban; it is a comparison. “Let the prophet who has a dream retell it, but let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” And then the word describes itself in terms Jeremiah's own bones already know: “Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?”

Nor can these prophets hide their workshop from Him. “Am I only a God nearby,” God asks, “and not a God far away?” “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” The chapter ends with a piece of slang dying in public. The people had taken to calling Jeremiah's oracles the burden of the LORD, as a joke at the prophet's expense, and God bans the phrase from the nation's mouth. Ask instead, “What has the LORD answered?” If the old phrase is used, the answer comes back as a sentence: “What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD.” The men who made a nickname out of God's word will be forgotten by God in return, He says, and brought to everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation. The shepherds scattered the flock. The prophets lied to it. The Branch and the gathering are God's answer to both.

title: Two Baskets of Figs
subtitle: Jeremiah 24
description: Two baskets before the temple sort the nation: good figs carried into exile, bad figs left behind with Zedekiah.
paragraphs: The setting of this vision is a deportation already completed. Nebuchadnezzar has carried Jeconiah, the officials of Judah, and the craftsmen and metalsmiths from Jerusalem to Babylon. The skilled and the governing are gone. And in front of the temple of the LORD, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs. One basket holds very good figs, the kind that ripen early and are prized. The other holds figs so bad they cannot be eaten. When God asks what he sees, Jeremiah reports it plainly: “The good figs are very good, but the bad figs are very bad, so bad they cannot be eaten.”

The interpretation reverses the obvious reading, and the reversal is the point of the vision. The good figs are not the people safe in Jerusalem. “Like these good figs, so I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.” The deported, the humiliated, the ones the homeland counts as finished, are the good produce. God even claims the deportation as His own act: He sent them away. What looks like Babylon's victory is, in the vision, God's husbandry, moving the good figs out of the basket before the rot takes everything.

What God promises the exiles is the first chapter's commission with every verb turned toward mercy. “I will keep My eyes on them for good and will return them to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them.” At his call, Jeremiah was appointed to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant. In Babylon, God says, the building and planting are underway, and the uprooting is suspended. And the deepest promise concerns the organ this book keeps diagnosing as deceitful and engraved with sin: “I will give them a heart to know Me, that I am the LORD. They will be My people, and I will be their God, for they will return to Me with all their heart.” The knowledge of God that chapter 22 defined as justice for the poor will be given to the exiles as a gift, in a foreign land, with a whole heart.

The bad basket is the shock the vision was built to deliver. “So will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem,” those remaining in the land and those who will flee to Egypt. The king still on David's throne, the court still functioning, the people who avoided deportation and congratulated themselves on staying home: inedible. “I will make them a horror and an offense to all the kingdoms of the earth, a disgrace and an object of scorn, ridicule, and cursing wherever I have banished them.” Sword, famine, and plague will run against them until they have perished from the land God gave their fathers. Staying in Jerusalem is not safety. In this vision it is the curse.

Two baskets redraw the map of the nation's future, and everything Jeremiah does from here on stands on this vision. The future of Judah is not in Jerusalem. It is on the road to Babylon, in the deportees' camps, among people who have lost everything except the eyes of God on them for good. That is why the prophet will soon write a letter to the exiles telling them to build houses and plant gardens in the enemy's city, and why, during the final siege, he will buy a field in a land about to fall. The good figs are already where God is working. The bad figs are still in the temple courts, assuring one another that the temple of the LORD is the only basket that matters.

title: Seventy Years
subtitle: Jeremiah 25
description: The sermon is dated and sealed: seventy years for Babylon's rule, then the cup of wrath poured for every nation in turn.
paragraphs: This chapter is dated, and the date turns it into a summary of a career. It is the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. Jeremiah stands before all the people of Judah and counts back. For twenty-three years, from the thirteenth year of Josiah to this day, “the word of the LORD has come to me, and I have spoken to you again and again, but you have not listened.” He was not the only voice. God sent all His servants the prophets again and again with the same message: turn from your evil ways and deeds, dwell in the land, do not follow other gods, do not provoke God with the works of your hands. The answer across twenty-three years, from two generations of hearers, is the sentence that governs the chapter: you have not listened.

So the sentence is pronounced, and it contains the book's most startling title for a pagan king. God will summon the families of the north, “and I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon,” and bring him against this land and all the surrounding nations. My servant: the emperor who will burn the temple does his work, in Jeremiah's vocabulary, as God's employee. The land will be devoted to destruction, an object of horror and contempt. And the sounds go again, the full catalog this time: “Moreover, I will banish from them the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the lamp.” Millstones and lamplight are not festivals. They are breakfast and evening, daily life itself, switched off. “And this whole land will become a desolate wasteland, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years.”

The number is the chapter's gift to everyone who hears it: the domination has a term. “But when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation, the land of the Chaldeans, for their guilt, declares the LORD, and I will make it an everlasting desolation.” God's servant will be judged for the very work he was summoned to do, because of the guilt in how he did it. And the judgment is already text. God will bring on Babylon “all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah has prophesied against all the nations.” The sermons have become a book, and the book has an expiry date for empires. Both halves matter. Babylon's power is real, and Babylon's power is scheduled.

Then the sermon becomes a ceremony. “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it.” “And they will drink and stagger and go out of their minds, because of the sword that I will send among them.” Jeremiah obeys in the vision as he obeyed in the streets: “So I took the cup from the LORD’s hand and made all the nations drink from it.” The list of drinkers runs outward from home. Jerusalem and the cities of Judah drink first, then Pharaoh and Egypt, the Philistine cities, Edom and Moab and the Ammonites, Tyre and Sidon, the kings of Arabia, Elam and Media, all the kings of the north near and far. And the last name on the list is a coded one: “And after all of them, the king of Sheshach will drink it too.” Sheshach is Babylon under a cipher, as the chapters on Babylon will confirm. The empire that pours for everyone else drinks last, and drinks the same cup.

If any nation refuses the cup, Jeremiah is to close the argument with a single piece of logic. “You most certainly must drink it!” “For behold, I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name, so how could you possibly go unpunished?” Judgment begins at God's own address; nobody downstream is exempt. The chapter ends with the sound of the judge arriving. “The LORD will roar from on high; He will raise His voice from His holy habitation. He will roar loudly over His pasture.” The shepherds of the nations are told to wail and roll in the dust: “Wail, you shepherds, and cry out; roll in the dust, you leaders of the flock. For the days of your slaughter have come.” And the shepherd image gives way to the oldest one in the book. “He has left His den like a lion, for their land has been made a desolation by the sword of the oppressor, and because of the fierce anger of the LORD.” The lion from the thicket has a name now, and a term of service, and a cup of his own waiting at the end of the list.

title: On Trial for His Life
subtitle: Jeremiah 26
description: The temple sermon is retried as a capital case, and the elders save Jeremiah with the hundred-year-old precedent of Micah.
paragraphs: The book steps back again, to the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, years before the seventy-years sermon, and the scene is the temple sermon preached a second time under orders that leave nothing out. “Stand in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and speak all the words I have commanded you to speak to all the cities of Judah who come to worship there. Do not omit a word.” And God states His reason for the completeness, and it is a reason Jeremiah has heard before in the potter's house: “Perhaps they will listen and turn,” each from his evil way, “so that I may relent of the disaster I am planning to bring upon them because of the evil of their deeds.” The threat Jeremiah is sent to deliver is, in God's own framing, an offer. “Then I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth.”

Jeremiah delivers every word, and as soon as he finishes, the priests and prophets and all the people seize him in the house of the LORD. Their shout is the charge and the sentence in one breath: “You must surely die!” “How dare you prophesy in the name of the LORD that this house will become like Shiloh and this city will be desolate and deserted!” The officials of Judah hear the uproar and come up from the palace and take their seats at the entrance of the New Gate, and the mob becomes a court. The prosecution states its case in a single sentence. “This man is worthy of death, for he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears!”

Jeremiah's defense is four sentences long and he makes no attempt to soften any of it. “The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard.” He does not retract the sermon; he repeats its offer in the courtroom: “So now, correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God, so that He might relent of the disaster He has pronounced against you.” Then he surrenders himself without surrendering the message. “As for me, here I am in your hands; do to me what you think is good and right.” And he attaches one warning to his own execution: “But know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents; for truly the LORD has sent me to speak all these words in your hearing.” The officials and all the people turn to the priests and prophets and deliver the verdict: “This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!”

Then some of the elders of the land stand up and do something nobody else in the book does: they cite precedent, and the precedent is another prophet. A century earlier, Micah the Moreshite had preached this same sermon in the days of Hezekiah, in words this series has already heard in Micah's own book: “Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount a wooded ridge.” The elders put the comparison to the assembly. “Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death? Did Hezekiah not fear the LORD and seek His favor, and did not the LORD relent of the disaster He had pronounced against them?” Hezekiah heard the identical threat, trembled, sought God's favor, and lived, and Micah lived. The elders close the argument on the court itself: we are about to bring great harm on ourselves.

The chapter refuses to let the rescue stand as the whole story. There was another man prophesying the same things at the same time: Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. King Jehoiakim sought his death, Uriah fled to Egypt, and the king sent Elnathan son of Achbor to bring him back. They brought Uriah out of Egypt, and Jehoiakim had him put to the sword and his body thrown into the burial place of the common people. Same sermon, same city, same years. One prophet had elders and a king who feared the LORD a century earlier; the other had neither. The difference between Jeremiah's outcome and Uriah's is stated in the chapter's final verse, and it is a man's hand, not a principle: “Nevertheless, Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death.” Remember the name of Ahikam's son. He will govern what is left of Judah, and Jeremiah will live in his house after the fall.

title: Yokes of Wood and Iron
subtitle: Jeremiah 27-28
description: Jeremiah wears a yoke before the nations' envoys, Hananiah breaks it in the temple, and God replaces the wood with iron.
paragraphs: At the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, Jerusalem hosts a war council. Envoys from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon have come to Zedekiah to plan a rebellion against Babylon, and God sends Jeremiah into the middle of the diplomacy wearing the argument on his own body. “Make for yourself a yoke out of leather straps and put it on your neck.” Each envoy is to carry God's message home to his king, and the message begins at creation. “By My great power and outstretched arm, I made the earth and the men and beasts on the face of it, and I give it to whom I please.” The earth is God's to assign, and He has assigned it. “So now I have placed all these lands under the authority of My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. I have even made the beasts of the field subject to him.”

The assignment has the same limit the seventy-years sermon set. “All nations will serve him and his son and grandson, until the time of his own land comes; then many nations and great kings will enslave him.” Within the term, the choice for each nation is brutally practical. Resistance means punishment by sword and famine and plague until Babylon destroys it. Submission means survival at home: “But the nation that will put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serve him, I will leave in its own land, to cultivate it and reside in it, declares the LORD.” Jeremiah speaks the same message to Zedekiah in the palace: “Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon; serve him and his people, and live!” “Why should you and your people die by sword and famine and plague”?

Against this stand the war council's own prophets, diviners, dream interpreters, mediums, and sorcerers, and their message is the alliance's platform: “You will not serve the king of Babylon.” In Jerusalem the temple prophets add a religious version of the same hope: “Look, very soon now the articles from the house of the LORD will be brought back from Babylon.” Jeremiah answers that the articles are going the other way. The pillars, the sea, the bases, everything Nebuchadnezzar left behind when he took Jeconiah, will follow Jeconiah east. “They will be carried to Babylon and will remain there until the day I attend to them again,” God says. “Then I will bring them back and restore them to this place.” Even the temple furniture gets an exile and a return date. The lie says soon and means never. The word says carried away, and means it, and adds the return.

In the fifth month of Zedekiah's fourth year, the argument becomes theatre. Hananiah son of Azzur, a prophet from Gibeon, confronts Jeremiah in the house of the LORD before the priests and all the people and preaches the counter-sermon in God's name. “I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.” “Within two years I will restore to this place all the articles of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon removed from here and carried to Babylon.” Jeconiah and all the exiles are coming home inside the same two years. Jeremiah's reply, before the whole crowd, is the most surprising sentence in the chapter: “May the LORD do so! May the LORD fulfill the words you have prophesied, and may He restore the articles of His house and all the exiles back to this place from Babylon.” He wants Hananiah to be right. Then he states the test that history applies to peace prophets. “The prophets of old who preceded you and me prophesied war, disaster, and plague against many lands and great kingdoms.” “As for the prophet who prophesies peace, only if the word of the prophet comes true will the prophet be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent.” Hananiah answers the test by taking the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaking it before all the people: “In this way, within two years I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon off the neck of all the nations.” Jeremiah does not answer. He goes on his way.

The word comes to him afterward, privately, and it is an upgrade of the sentence, not a repeal. “You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron.” “I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations to make them serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and they will serve him.” Hananiah's broken prop has made the real bondage heavier for every nation that believed him. Jeremiah delivers the rest of the word to Hananiah's face: “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie.” “I am about to remove you from the face of the earth. You will die this year because you have preached rebellion against the LORD.” The chapter's last line is a date. “And in the seventh month of that very year, the prophet Hananiah died.” Two months after the broken yoke, the peace prophet is in the ground, and the iron yoke is still on every neck in the region.

title: The Letter to the Exiles
subtitle: Jeremiah 29
description: Jeremiah writes to Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, seek the city's welfare, and do not listen to your prophets there.
paragraphs: What Jeremiah could not get Jerusalem to hear, he puts in writing and sends to Babylon. The letter goes to the surviving elders among the exiles and to the priests, the prophets, and all the people Nebuchadnezzar carried away, and it travels in the diplomatic pouch of Zedekiah's own envoys, Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah. Its opening orders would have sounded like surrender in Jerusalem and like sabotage to the exiles' own prophets. “Build houses and settle down. Plant gardens and eat their produce.” “Take wives and have sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they too may have sons and daughters. Multiply there; do not decrease.” Not tents. Not a protest camp. Houses, gardens, weddings, grandchildren.

Then the order that has echoed through every exile since: “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.” The exiles are to pray for Babylon, the city that burned their temple, because their welfare is tied to its welfare for the duration. The prophets among them are preaching a short exile and an imminent return, and Jeremiah warns them not to be deceived by the dreams they keep eliciting. The term God set stands, and the letter attaches the promise to the term: “When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place.”

Inside that frame stands the sentence this letter is famous for, and the frame is part of the sentence. “For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.” The you is plural, a people, not a private address. The plans run on God's calendar, not the exiles': first the seventy years, then the attending, the prayer heard, the seeking rewarded. “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.” “I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore you from captivity and gather you from all the nations and places to which I have banished you.” Most of the letter's first readers would die in Babylon with the promise unfulfilled in their own lifetimes. The future and the hope were real, and they were addressed to the people's survival across the full length of the exile. The letter asks its readers to build houses their grandchildren will inherit in a land they themselves will not see again, and to call that God's good plan.

For the brothers who stayed home, the letter carries the figs vision as policy. The king on David's throne and the people who did not go into exile will be made “like rotten figs, so bad they cannot be eaten,” pursued by sword and famine and plague into horror among the nations. Exile is the mercy. Staying is the sentence. And inside Babylon itself, Jeremiah names the two local prophets preaching the short exile, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah: “I will deliver them to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will kill them before your very eyes.” Their names become a curse formula among the exiles: “May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire!”

The letter also produces a counter-letter. Shemaiah the Nehelamite writes from Babylon to Jerusalem, to the priest Zephaniah and all the priests, demanding to know why the temple authorities have not done their duty against the madman Jeremiah of Anathoth: “you must put him in stocks and neck irons.” His evidence is the letter itself, which he quotes back to Jerusalem as the crime: “Since the exile will be lengthy, build houses and settle down; plant gardens and eat their produce.” The priest Zephaniah, holding a letter that demands Jeremiah be stocked, reads it aloud to Jeremiah instead. Jeremiah's answering word goes out to all the exiles: “I will surely punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite and his descendants. He will have no one left among this people, nor will he see the good that I will bring to My people, declares the LORD, for he has preached rebellion against the LORD.” The good the letter promises will happen. The man who fought the letter will not be there to see it. The exile has its instructions now, written down and delivered: settle, multiply, pray for the city, and count the years.

title: Write It in a Book
subtitle: Jeremiah 30
description: The book of consolation opens with a writing command, an incurable wound, and a promise that Jacob's trouble ends in rest.
paragraphs: The next four chapters are set apart in the book itself, and they run against everything around them. God tells Jeremiah to bind the consolation the way the judgments were bound: “Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you.” The book opens with its destination stated in advance: “For behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will restore from captivity My people Israel and Judah, declares the LORD. I will restore them to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they will possess it.” Israel and Judah both, the divorced north and the falling south, named together as one people with one restoration. But the consolation does not skip the disaster to reach it. The first sounds in the book are panic.

“A cry of panic is heard,” God says, a cry of terror, not of peace. Every man stands with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor, and every face has turned pale. “How awful that day will be! None will be like it! It is the time of Jacob’s distress, but he will be saved out of it.” The book of comfort begins inside the birth pangs, not after them. What is born through the distress is stated in the next breath, in terms that answer the iron yoke of the Hananiah years: “On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will break the yoke off their necks and tear off their bonds, and no longer will strangers enslave them.” “Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.” A king from David, raised up by God, in place of the enrolled-childless line. The yoke comes off by the same authority that put it on.

To the people inside the distress, God's word is the one thing He has been refusing to say to Jerusalem's defenders: do not be afraid. “As for you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, declares the LORD, and do not be dismayed, O Israel. For I will surely save you out of a distant place, your descendants from the land of their captivity!” The salvation is real, and so is the discipline inside it, and the chapter holds the two in a single distinction that runs through the whole consolation: “Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have scattered you, I will not completely destroy you. Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” The nations used as the rod are destroyed completely. The people disciplined by the rod are not. Completely is the border between them.

Then the wound from the balm sermon returns, with its diagnosis unchanged. “Your injury is incurable; your wound is grievous.” “There is no one to plead your cause, no remedy for your sores, no recovery for you.” All her lovers have forgotten her and no longer seek her, and the striking itself is God's: “for I have struck you as an enemy would, with the discipline of someone cruel, because of your great iniquity and your numerous sins.” No physician in Gilead could touch this wound because God is the one who gave it. And that is exactly why the next verse can say what no physician could: “Nevertheless, all who devour you will be devoured.” “Those who plundered you will be plundered, and all who raided you will be raided.” “But I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD, because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares.” The balm question gets its answer at last, from the striker Himself: the health of the daughter of God's people will be restored by the hand that wounded her, and the name the nations sneer, outcast Zion, is the name in the promise.

The rebuilding is pictured at ground level. “I will restore the fortunes of Jacob’s tents and have compassion on his dwellings. And the city will be rebuilt on her own ruins, and the palace will stand in its rightful place.” On her own ruins: not relocated, not replaced, rebuilt where she fell. “Thanksgiving will proceed from them, a sound of celebration.” Their children will be as in days of old, and their ruler one of their own: “Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst.” And the covenant formula that opened the nation's story is spoken over the tents: “And you will be My people, and I will be your God.” The chapter closes with the storm oracle repeated from the prophets chapter, God's fury going out against the wicked, and one line of patience inside it: “In the days to come you will understand this.” Understanding is promised. It is just scheduled later than everyone wants it.

title: Rachel Weeping, and a New Covenant
subtitle: Jeremiah 31
description: Rachel weeps at Ramah and is answered, road markers are set for the way home, and a new covenant is promised with the law on the heart.
paragraphs: This chapter is the heart of the consolation, and it begins before there was a nation to console. “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion.” The love is older than the exile and will outlast it. Its first picture is a woman restored to celebration: “Again I will build you, and you will be rebuilt, O Virgin Israel. Again you will take up your tambourines and go out in joyful dancing.” Vineyards return to the hills of Samaria, the northern hills, enemy territory for two centuries. And on those hills the watchmen, whose job was to warn of armies, get a new call to cry: “Arise, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God!” The return God describes is not an able-bodied march. “Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north and gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, including the blind and the lame, expectant mothers and women in labor. They will return as a great assembly!” The slowest and weakest are named in the manifest.

“They will come with weeping, and by their supplication I will lead them; I will make them walk beside streams of waters, on a level path where they will not stumble. For I am Israel’s Father, and Ephraim is My firstborn.” The scattering God takes personal credit for reversing: “The One who scattered Israel will gather them and keep them as a shepherd keeps his flock.” On the heights of Zion they will be radiant over grain and new wine and oil, and “their life will be like a well-watered garden, and never again will they languish.” “I will turn their mourning into joy, and give them comfort and joy for their sorrow.” It is the tree of the earlier sermon, planted by the waters, now grown into a whole people's landscape.

But before the joy settles, a voice interrupts from Ramah, the town north of Jerusalem where grief has a family name. “A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.” Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps from her tomb over children who are gone. And God answers the dead mother as if she could hear Him: “Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears, for the reward for your work will come, declares the LORD. Then your children will return from the land of the enemy.” “So there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children will return to their own land.” Then the northern son himself is overheard repenting. Ephraim's moaning is quoted in full: “You disciplined me severely, like an untrained calf. Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God.” After he returned, he says, he repented; after he was instructed, he struck his thigh in grief, ashamed of the disgrace of his youth. God's response is not a lecture. It is a father's inventory of his feelings: “Is not Ephraim a precious son to Me, a delightful child? Though I often speak against him, I still remember him. Therefore My heart yearns for him; I have great compassion for him.”

The road home gets signage. “Set up the road markers, put up the signposts. Keep the highway in mind, the road you have traveled. Return, O Virgin Israel, return to these cities of yours.” Jeremiah wakes from the vision like a man from good sleep and says so: “My sleep had been most pleasant to me.” And then the watching wordplay of his call comes back fulfilled. The God who was watching over His word to uproot now pledges the other half of the shepherd's staff: “Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down, to demolish, destroy, and bring disaster, so I will watch over them to build and to plant.” Even the proverb of blame is retired in those days. No more the fathers eating sour grapes and the children's teeth set on edge; each will die for his own iniquity.

Then, without transition, the chapter gives the promise by which it is known to the world. “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” “It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt,” the covenant “they broke, though I was a husband to them.” “But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.” The law moves from stone and scroll to mind and heart, the same hearts this book has called deceitful and engraved with sin. Its result is a world where nobody needs to be told to know the LORD, “because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest,” and its foundation is a sentence about God's memory: “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.” The guarantee on the whole covenant is the sky's own reliability: “Only if this fixed order departed from My presence, declares the LORD, would Israel’s descendants ever cease to be a nation before Me.” And the chapter ends by measuring the rebuilt city, tower of Hananel to Corner Gate, and consecrating the ground nobody thought could ever be holy: “The whole valley of the dead bodies and ashes, and all the fields as far as the Kidron Valley, to the corner of the Horse Gate to the east, will be holy to the LORD. It will never again be uprooted or demolished.” The valley of the corpses, holy. That is where the new covenant sermon stops.

title: The Field at Anathoth
subtitle: Jeremiah 32
description: While the siege closes in, Jeremiah buys his cousin's field at Anathoth and jars the deed, because fields will be bought in the land again.
paragraphs: The date is the siege itself: the tenth year of Zedekiah, the eighteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, with Babylon's army around Jerusalem and Jeremiah imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard in the palace. Zedekiah's charge against him is a quotation of his own sermons: you claim the LORD will deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, that Zedekiah will not escape but will speak with the king face to face and see him eye to eye, that fighting the Chaldeans cannot succeed. Into that courtyard, mid-siege, comes a piece of family business the LORD announced in advance. Jeremiah's cousin Hanamel, son of his uncle Shallum, arrives to exercise a right out of the old land law. “Buy for yourself my field in Anathoth, for you have the right of redemption to buy it.” When Hanamel stands in the courtyard saying it, “Please buy my field in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for you own the right of inheritance and redemption. Buy it for yourself,” Jeremiah records his own recognition: “Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.”

So the prophet buys a field in a country being overrun, inside a city about to fall, with an enemy army between him and the land. And he does the transaction with exaggerated, deliberate legality. He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver on the scales. He signs the deed and seals it and calls in witnesses. There are two copies, the sealed copy with its terms and conditions and the open copy, and both are handed to Baruch son of Neriah in front of Hanamel, the witnesses, and every Jew sitting in the courtyard of the guard. The instruction Baruch carries is the point of the whole ceremony: take these deeds “and put them in a clay jar to preserve them for a long time.” Clay jars outlast sieges. Then the word that interprets the act: “Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.” The purchase is a prophecy performed in paperwork. As long as that jar sits unopened somewhere in the ruins, the future of real estate in Judah is a settled fact.

Then Jeremiah prays, and the prayer is honest in a way that makes it famous. It begins with the doctrine: “Oh, Lord GOD! You have made the heavens and the earth by Your great power and outstretched arm. Nothing is too difficult for You!” It walks through the loving devotion shown to thousands, the signs and wonders in Egypt, the gift of the land flowing with milk and honey, and the people's refusal to obey, right up to the siege ramps mounted against the city. And then the prayer turns its doctrine on itself. You told me to buy the field with silver and call in witnesses, he says, “even though the city has been delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans!” The prayer is a man asking God how the promise and the ramps can both be true at the same time.

God's answer starts by handing the doctrine back: “Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is anything too difficult for Me?” Then, before any comfort, the judgment is restated in full, because the field does not repeal the sentence. The Chaldeans will burn the city and the rooftop shrines with it. The people turned their backs and not their faces, though God taught them again and again. They set their abominations in the house that bears His name and built the high places of Baal in the Valley of Ben-hinnom to pass their children through the fire to Molech, a thing God says, for the third time in this book, He never commanded, “nor had it ever entered My mind.” The city of which everyone says it will be delivered into Babylon's hand by sword and famine and plague: that city, God says, is the one He is talking about next.

“I will surely gather My people from all the lands to which I have banished them in My furious anger and great wrath, and I will return them to this place and make them dwell in safety.” “They will be My people, and I will be their God.” “I will give them one heart and one way, so that they will always fear Me for their own good and for the good of their children after them.” Then the covenant, in terms stronger than the sermon's needs: “I will make an everlasting covenant with them: I will never turn away from doing good to them, and I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me.” And at the center of the answer stands a sentence about God's own emotions that has no equal in the prophets for plainness: “Yes, I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will faithfully plant them in this land with all My heart and with all My soul.” In Zephaniah, a generation earlier in this series, God sang over His people. Here He does business with them in joy, planting them with His whole heart and soul. The symmetry God claims for Himself closes the answer: “Just as I have brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring on them all the good I have promised them.” And the final picture is the courtyard ceremony multiplied across the map: “Fields will be purchased with silver, and deeds will be signed, sealed, and witnessed in the land of Benjamin,” in the hill country, the foothills, the Negev, because God will restore them from captivity. Jeremiah's seventeen shekels were the first installment.

title: Call to Me
subtitle: Jeremiah 33
description: From the prison court comes the invitation: call to Me and I will answer you, and tell you great and hidden things.
paragraphs: Jeremiah is still confined in the courtyard of the guard when the word comes a second time. The introduction names the speaker with creator's credentials, and then the invitation that gives this sermon its name: “Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know.” The things are shown against the immediate landscape: the houses of the city and the palaces of the kings of Judah torn down for defense against the siege ramps and the sword, their rooms to be filled with the corpses of men God will strike down in His anger, in a city He has hidden His face from. That is the present tense. The sentence that follows begins with the book's great reversal word: “Nevertheless, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people and reveal to them the abundance of peace and truth.”

The healing is moral before it is medical. “And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me.” The incurable wound of the consolation's first chapter is now scheduled for cleansing by the one who inflicted it. And the city whose name has been a byword gets a new reputation among the nations: “So this city will bring Me renown, joy, praise, and glory before all the nations of the earth, who will hear of all the good I do for it.” They will tremble, God says, because of the goodness and prosperity He provides for it. Jerusalem as a source of awe for the wrong reasons has filled this book. Here she fills the nations with awe for the opposite reason.

Then come the sounds, and readers of this book have heard them before, in their absence. The temple sermon removed the sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of the bride and bridegroom from the streets. The seventy-years sermon removed them again, with the millstones and the lamplight. In the courtyard sermon, the sentence is repealed item by item. In the place everyone calls a wasteland without man or beast, “there will be heard again” “the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom,” and the voices of worshipers bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD with the shout on their lips: “Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever.” The desolate places will hold shepherds' pastures again, and in Benjamin and the hill country and the Negev “the flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.” Ordinary life, counted sheep by sheep, is treated as a headline promise.

The Branch returns, and with him comes a transfer of the book's most famous name. “In those days and at that time I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch, and He will administer justice and righteousness in the land.” “In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.” In chapter 23 the name belonged to the King. Here it is given to the city: what the King is, the city under him becomes. And the institutions that fell with the kings are guaranteed alongside him: “David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,” “nor will the priests who are Levites ever fail to have a man before Me to offer burnt offerings.”

The guarantee God offers for all of it is the calendar itself. “If you can break My covenant with the day and My covenant with the night, so that day and night cease to occupy their appointed time,” then, and only then, “My covenant may also be broken with David My servant and with My ministers the Levites who are priests.” Break sunrise first, God says, and then we can talk about breaking this. The sermon closes by answering a proverb of despair already circulating among the people, who have begun to say it as settled fact: “The LORD has rejected the two families He had chosen.” God's reply runs through the fixed order of heaven and earth and ends on a word this book has taught its readers to watch for: “For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them.” The consolation is complete. The siege outside the courtyard is not, and the book turns back to it.

title: Freedom Taken Back
subtitle: Jeremiah 34
description: Jerusalem frees its Hebrew slaves by covenant under siege, then takes the freedom back, and God proclaims a liberty of another kind.
paragraphs: This word comes during the final assault, when Nebuchadnezzar's whole coalition is fighting Jerusalem and the only fortified cities left in Judah are Lachish and Azekah. Jeremiah is sent to Zedekiah one more time, and the message has two halves. The city will fall: “Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it down.” Zedekiah will not escape; he will see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face and go to Babylon. But for the king personally there is a clause of mercy inside the sentence: “Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah. This is what the LORD says concerning you: You will not die by the sword; you will die in peace.” Spices will be burned for him as for the kings before him, and the mourners will lament him with the royal refrain: “Alas, O master!” Jeremiah delivers all of it in Jerusalem while the fighting is underway.

Then the city does something it has never done in this book: it obeys, publicly and completely, for a while. After Zedekiah makes a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty, every master is to free his Hebrew slaves, male and female, and no one is to hold his fellow Jew in bondage. The release was not an invention of the siege. It was an old command with a calendar on it, and the whole city signs on. All the officials and all the people who entered into the covenant agree to free their menservants and maidservants and no longer hold them in bondage. They obeyed, the text says, and released them. For one season in the last months of the kingdom, Jerusalem does exactly what God asks, in the house that bears His name.

And then they reverse it. The Babylonian army withdraws for a time to meet an Egyptian advance, the pressure lifts, and the masters change their minds. They take back the menservants and maidservants they had freed and force them to become slaves again. God's review of the episode reads like a court record. “I made a covenant with your forefathers when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,” with the seventh-year release written into it. “But your fathers did not listen or incline their ear.” This generation almost broke the pattern: “Recently you repented and did what pleased Me; each of you proclaimed freedom for his neighbor. You made a covenant before Me in the house that bears My Name.” “But now you have changed your minds and profaned My name. Each of you has taken back the menservants and maidservants whom you had set at liberty to go wherever they wanted, and you have again forced them to be your slaves.”

God answers their proclamation with a proclamation of His own, built from the same word. “You have not obeyed Me; you have not proclaimed freedom, each man for his brother and for his neighbor. So now I proclaim freedom for you, declares the LORD,” and the freedom He proclaims is “freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!” They would not set their brothers free to live. They are set free themselves, to the three destroyers who have ridden through this whole book. The covenant ritual they performed turns into the instrument of the sentence. They had cut a calf in two and passed between its pieces, accepting the curse of the covenant on themselves if they broke it. God calls in the ritual's own terms: “those who have transgressed My covenant and have not fulfilled the terms of the covenant they made before Me, I will treat like the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces.” The officials, the priests, and all the people who walked between the pieces will be delivered to their enemies, and their corpses will feed the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.

The last word concerns the army that left. “Behold, I am going to give the command, declares the LORD, and I will bring them back to this city. They will fight against it, capture it, and burn it down.” The reprieve was never a rescue; it was the interval in which Jerusalem revealed itself. With Egypt marching and Babylon gone, the city had one free choice to make in its final year, and it used its freedom to re-enslave its brothers. That is the act this chapter sets at the head of the fall: not the idolatry of the fathers, not Manasseh, but a kindness performed before God in His house and then, when it cost something, taken back.

title: The Rechabites and the Burned Scroll
subtitle: Jeremiah 35-36
description: The Rechabites keep a dead father's command for 250 years; Jehoiakim burns the scroll column by column, and God dictates it again, with additions.
paragraphs: The book steps back again, to the days of Jehoiakim, for two stories about obedience, one from a clan nobody in Jerusalem can imitate and one from a king who will not even listen. God sends Jeremiah to the house of the Rechabites, a clan that lived by the rules of an ancestor, and has him bring the whole family into a chamber of the house of the LORD, near the officials' rooms, and set pitchers full of wine and cups in front of them. Drink some wine, Jeremiah says. The Rechabites refuse, in formation: “We do not drink wine.” Their reason is a command from a dead man. Their forefather Jonadab son of Rechab ordered his descendants: “Neither you nor your descendants are ever to drink wine.” “Nor are you ever to build a house or sow seed or plant a vineyard. Those things are not for you. Instead, you must live in tents all your lives, so that you may live a long time in the land where you wander.”

Then the clan gives its own report, and it is a record-keeping more exact than any king's in this book. “And we have obeyed the voice of our forefather Jonadab son of Rechab in all he commanded us.” No wine for anyone, wives and sons and daughters included. No houses built. No vineyards, fields, or crops owned. “But we have lived in tents and have obeyed and done exactly as our forefather Jonadab commanded us.” The only reason tent-dwellers are inside Jerusalem's walls at all is the invasion: when Nebuchadnezzar marched into the land, they came into the city to escape the Chaldean and Aramean armies. God's application is the reason for the wine test: “Will you not accept discipline and obey My words?” “The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out. He commanded his sons not to drink wine, and they have not drunk it to this very day because they have obeyed the command of their forefather. But I have spoken to you again and again, and you have not obeyed Me!” A human forefather's command, carried across generations of descendants who never met him, is kept without exception. The living God, speaking again and again through prophet after prophet, cannot get one generation to listen. The Rechabites receive a promise no king in this book receives: “Jonadab son of Rechab will never fail to have a man to stand before Me.”

In Jehoiakim's fourth year, God commissions the book itself. “Take a scroll and write on it all the words I have spoken to you concerning Israel, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I first spoke to you during the reign of Josiah until today.” The purpose is the purpose of the trial sermon: “Perhaps when the people of Judah hear about all the calamity I plan to bring upon them, each of them will turn from his wicked way. Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.” Jeremiah cannot enter the temple himself: “I am restricted; I cannot enter the house of the LORD.” So Baruch son of Neriah takes the dictation, ink on scroll, and on the fast day, in the chamber of Gemariah the scribe, in the hearing of all the people, Baruch reads the whole of Jeremiah's career aloud.

The scroll moves upward through the government like a fire alarm. Micaiah, Gemariah's son, hears it and reports it to the officials in the palace. They summon Baruch, sit him down, and hear it again, and turn to one another in fear: “Surely we must report all these words to the king.” They ask how the scroll was made, and Baruch's answer is the method of the whole book: “It was at his dictation,” Baruch replied. “He recited all these words to me and I wrote them in ink on the scroll.” The officials hide the two men, store the scroll in Elishama's chamber, and report everything to the king. Jehoiakim, in his winter quarters in the ninth month with a fire burning before him, has Jehudi read it. As each three or four columns are read, the king cuts them off with a scribe's knife and throws them into the firepot, until the entire scroll is consumed. “Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments.” Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah beg him not to burn it. He will not listen. He orders Baruch and Jeremiah seized, “but the LORD had hidden them.”

The answer to the burning arrives as a writing assignment. “Take another scroll and rewrite on it the very words that were on the original scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah has burned.” Jehoiakim's own sentence is folded into the rewrite: “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne, and his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night,” the donkey burial of the palace sermon confirmed against the king who burned its record. And the chapter's last verse is the book describing its own survival: “Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah, and at Jeremiah’s dictation he wrote on it all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.” The fire did not shorten the book. It lengthened it.

title: The Cistern and the Secret King
subtitle: Jeremiah 37-38
description: Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter, lowered into a mud cistern, lifted out on ropes padded with rags, and summoned to a secret audience.
paragraphs: Zedekiah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar in place of Coniah, never obeys the prophet he keeps consulting. “But he and his officers and the people of the land refused to obey the words that the LORD had spoken through Jeremiah the prophet.” Yet when Pharaoh's army marches out of Egypt and the Chaldeans lift the siege to meet it, the king sends Jehucal and the priest Zephaniah to Jeremiah with the familiar request: “Please pray to the LORD our God for us!” Jeremiah is still a free man at this point, coming and going among the people. The answer to the prayer request is the opposite of the relief the court is celebrating. “Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which has marched out to help you, will go back to its own land of Egypt.” “Then the Chaldeans will return and fight against this city. They will capture it and burn it down.” God adds a picture to close every loophole of hope: “Indeed, if you were to strike down the entire army of the Chaldeans that is fighting against you, and only wounded men remained in their tents, they would still get up and burn this city down.”

During the lull, Jeremiah starts out of the city toward the land of Benjamin to claim his portion there among his people, an ordinary property errand of the kind he once performed for Hanamel in reverse. At the Gate of Benjamin, the captain of the guard, Irijah son of Shelemiah, seizes him on a capital charge: “You are deserting to the Chaldeans!” “That is a lie,” Jeremiah replied. “I am not deserting to the Chaldeans!” Irijah will not listen. The officials are angry, beat him, and jail him in the house of Jonathan the scribe, which had been converted into a prison. “So Jeremiah went into a cell in the dungeon and remained there a long time.” Then the king who would not rescue him publicly sends for him privately. “Is there a word from the LORD?” “You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.” Jeremiah uses the audience to plead his own case: “How have I sinned against you or your servants or these people, that you have put me in prison?” Where are the king's prophets now, the ones who promised Babylon would never come? His petition is for his life, and it is modest: “But now please listen, O my lord the king. May my petition come before you. Do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, or I will die there.” Zedekiah moves him to the courtyard of the guard and orders him “a loaf of bread daily from the street of the bakers, until all the bread in the city was gone.”

From the courtyard Jeremiah keeps preaching the surrender sermon to all the people, and four officials, Shephatiah, Gedaliah son of Pashhur, Jucal, and Pashhur son of Malchijah, bring the king a demand: “This man ought to die, for he is discouraging the warriors who remain in this city, as well as all the people, by speaking such words to them; this man is not seeking the well-being of these people, but their ruin.” The king of Judah answers like a man describing the weather: “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.” They take Jeremiah to the cistern of Malchiah the king's son, in the courtyard of the guard, and lower him by ropes into it. “They lowered Jeremiah with ropes into the cistern, which had no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud.” There is no more bread in the city. He will starve in the mud if the mud does not finish him first, and no Judahite official objects.

The objection comes from a Cushite. Ebed-melech, a court official from Ethiopia, hears what has been done and goes to the king at the Gate of Benjamin and says it to his face: “My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet. They have dropped him into the cistern, where he will starve to death, for there is no more bread in the city.” Zedekiah, who could do nothing to stop four officials, can do this: he gives Ebed-melech thirty men and an order to pull Jeremiah out before he dies. Ebed-melech goes to a place below the storehouse in the palace and collects old rags and worn-out clothes, and lowers them with the ropes and a piece of practical mercy: “Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes.” They pull the prophet up out of the mud, and Jeremiah remains in the courtyard of the guard. The man who saved Jeremiah's life in the last days of Jerusalem is a foreigner with a pile of rags, and this book does not let his name be lost.

Zedekiah sends for Jeremiah a third time, to the third entrance of the house of the LORD, and opens with a request for candor. Jeremiah states his terms first: “If I tell you,” Jeremiah replied, “you will surely put me to death. And even if I give you advice, you will not listen to me.” The king swears secretly: “As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” Then the word comes, the same word, for the last time: “If you indeed surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.” “But if you do not surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then this city will be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans. They will burn it down, and you yourself will not escape their grasp.” Zedekiah finally names his reason, and it is not theology. It is fear of mockery from his own deserters: “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.” “They will not hand you over,” Jeremiah replied. “Obey the voice of the LORD in what I am telling you, that it may go well with you and you may live.” God shows Jeremiah what refusal looks like: the palace women carried out to Babylon's officials, singing over the king they are leaving, “They misled you and overcame you,” the trusted friends, and then, “Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.” The king in the mud of his own indecision, pictured in the mud Jeremiah was pulled from. Zedekiah's response to the last offer of his life is to arrange a cover story for the officials and swear the prophet to secrecy. “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.”

title: The Day Jerusalem Was Captured
subtitle: Jeremiah 39
description: Jerusalem falls in a chapter of plain record, and the spoil-of-war promise is paid by name to a prophet and a Cushite servant.
paragraphs: The fall is recorded the way a clerk records it, with dates. In the ninth year of Zedekiah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar marched against Jerusalem with his entire army and laid siege to the city. In Zedekiah's eleventh year, on the ninth day of the fourth month, the city was breached. The officials of the king of Babylon came in and sat down in the Middle Gate, the seat of judgment inside the captured city: Nergal-sharezer of Samgar, Nebo-sarsekim the Rabsaris, Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the rest. Babylon's court takes its seats in Jerusalem's gate, and the government of Judah is over.

Zedekiah runs. He and all the soldiers leave the city at night through the king's garden, by the gate between the two walls, heading for the Arabah. The Chaldeans overtake him in the plains of Jericho, the low ground where Israel once entered the land, and bring him up to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in the land of Hamath. Judgment is pronounced there, and it is executed in an order designed to be remembered by a man about to lose his eyes. The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and killed all the nobles of Judah. Then he put out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him with bronze chains to take him to Babylon. Everything Jeremiah had told this king came due in one afternoon. He would see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face: he did, at Riblah, in judgment. He would not die by the sword; he would die in Babylon, in chains and darkness, as a prisoner. The last sight Zedekiah's eyes ever held was the death of his sons.

In the city, the Chaldeans burned the palace and the houses of the people and broke down the walls. Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried the remnant of the people to Babylon, along with the deserters who had gone over to him. The surrender sermon had been right about who would live and how. And the land changed hands at the bottom: “But Nebuzaradan left behind in the land of Judah some of the poor people who had no property, and at that time he gave them vineyards and fields.” The poor who owned nothing receive vineyards and fields from the conqueror, in the land the kings and officials had filled with oppression. It is the only distribution of land in the chapter, and Babylon performs it.

Jeremiah's release is a matter of enemy standing orders. Nebuchadnezzar had given instructions about the prophet through Nebuzaradan: “Take him, look after him, and do not let any harm come to him; do for him whatever he says.” The captains of Babylon bring Jeremiah from the courtyard of the guard and hand him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, the hand that once saved him at his trial, now raised a generation later in Gedaliah, to take him home. “So Jeremiah remained among his own people.” The king of Babylon protects the prophet of God with a written order, after the kings of Judah protected him with stocks, a dungeon, and a cistern. The book does not comment on the comparison. It does not need to.

The chapter closes with a word spoken earlier, while Jeremiah was still confined, and addressed to the one man in the palace who had risked himself for the prophet. “Go and tell Ebed-melech the Cushite,” God says: “I am about to fulfill My words against this city for harm and not for good, and on that day they will be fulfilled before your eyes.” “But I will deliver you on that day, declares the LORD, and you will not be delivered into the hands of the men whom you fear.” “For I will surely rescue you so that you do not fall by the sword. Because you have trusted in Me, you will escape with your life like a spoil of war, declares the LORD.” The spoil-of-war promise was first made in this book to any common soldier or citizen who would walk out of the gates and surrender. Now it is paid, by name, to the Ethiopian official who padded the ropes with rags. The city has fallen exactly as preached for forty years, and the first two people the record shows God keeping are a prophet who would not stop preaching it and a foreigner who would not let him die in the mud.

title: The Governor at Mizpah
subtitle: Jeremiah 40-41
description: Gedaliah gathers the remnant at Mizpah and is murdered at his own table; the rescued captives camp at Geruth Chimham facing a decision of fear.
paragraphs: Jeremiah's freedom arrives by the strangest route in the book. After the fall, he is found at Ramah, the assembly point for the deportation, bound in chains among all the captives of Jerusalem and Judah being exiled to Babylon: the prophet swept up with the people he told to surrender. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, finds him there, and the captain of Babylon's guard preaches Jeremiah's whole ministry back to him in two sentences: “The LORD your God decreed this disaster on this place, and now the LORD has fulfilled it; He has done just as He said. Because you people have sinned against the LORD and have not obeyed His voice, this thing has happened to you.” Then the chains come off, and the conqueror makes the prisoner an offer no Judahite king ever made him: “But now, behold, I am freeing you today from the chains that were on your wrists. If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, then come, and I will take care of you. But if it seems wrong to you to come with me to Babylon, go no farther. Look, the whole land is before you. Wherever it seems good and right to you, go there.”

Jeremiah chooses home, such as it is. Nebuzaradan gives him a ration and a gift and steers him toward Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, the man Babylon has appointed over the cities of Judah, and Jeremiah goes to Mizpah and stays with him among the people left in the land. A remnant government assembles quickly. The army commanders still in the field come in with their men, Ishmael son of Nethaniah among them, and Gedaliah swears them an oath of safety: “Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you.” He will represent them at Mizpah before the Chaldeans; they are to “gather wine grapes, summer fruit, and oil, place them in your storage jars, and live in the cities you have taken.” Jews who had fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom, and every other land hear that a remnant exists and come home to it, “and they gathered an abundance of wine grapes and summer fruit.” For one harvest, the land works again under a governor Babylon appointed and Jeremiah's protector's son embodied: the surrendered life Jeremiah spent forty years prescribing, actually being lived.

Then Johanan son of Kareah comes to Gedaliah with intelligence: “Are you aware that Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?” Gedaliah does not believe him. Johanan asks privately for permission to kill Ishmael first, quietly, no one the wiser, rather than watch the remnant scatter and perish with its governor. Gedaliah forbids it outright: “Do not do such a thing! What you are saying about Ishmael is a lie.” It is the most decent sentence spoken by a ruler in the last chapters of the book, and it kills him. The governor who would not sanction a preemptive murder, who trusted the man at his own table, has signed his administration's death warrant with his integrity.

In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a member of the royal family and one of the king's chief officers, comes to Mizpah with ten men and eats a meal with Gedaliah. At the table, he and his men rise and strike Gedaliah down with the sword, and kill all the Jews who were with him, and the Chaldean soldiers stationed there. The next day, before the murder is known, eighty men arrive from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, beards shaved, garments torn, bodies cut in mourning, carrying grain offerings and frankincense for the house of the LORD, a house that stands in ruins. Ishmael goes out to meet them weeping as he comes, grief performed by the murderer, and invites them in: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” Inside the city he slaughters them and throws the bodies into a cistern. Ten of them buy their lives by disclosing hidden stores in the field: “Do not kill us, for we have hidden treasure in the field,” wheat and barley, oil and honey. The cistern Ishmael fills with the slain is a large one that King Asa had dug generations earlier for fear of Baasha king of Israel. A royal cistern built against an old siege becomes the mass grave of the remnant's first autumn.

Ishmael takes the rest captive, the king's daughters and everyone left at Mizpah, and sets out for the Ammonites who hired him. Johanan and the commanders pursue, and at the great pool in Gibeon the captives see their rescuers and rejoice and cross over to them wholesale. Ishmael escapes with eight men to the Ammonites. The rescued remnant camps at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to proceed into Egypt, because a murdered Babylonian governor means Chaldean reprisal, and everyone in the camp knows whose body will be found at Mizpah. The commonwealth of one harvest is over. The remnant that Jeremiah's preaching had assembled under Gedaliah is now a frightened caravan pointing itself at Egypt, and its next step is to ask the prophet a question it has already answered.

title: Whose Word Will Stand
subtitle: Jeremiah 42-44
description: The remnant swears to obey, waits ten days, hears stay, and marches to Egypt anyway, carrying Jeremiah to his last recorded sermon.
paragraphs: The whole remnant comes to Jeremiah in a body, commanders and people from the least to the greatest, with the most promising request anyone has made of him in the book. “May our petition come before you; pray to the LORD your God on behalf of this entire remnant.
