For few of us remain of the many, as you can see with your own eyes.” “Pray that the LORD your God will tell us the way we should walk and the thing we should do.” Jeremiah accepts on terms he states aloud: “I have heard you,” replied Jeremiah the prophet. “I will surely pray to the LORD your God as you request, and I will tell you everything that the LORD answers. I will not withhold a word from you.” And the remnant swears to the outcome in advance, calling God as its enforcement: “May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act upon every word that the LORD your God sends you to tell us.” “Whether it is pleasant or unpleasant, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God to whom we are sending you, so that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God!” Then everyone waits. The word takes ten days to come, and for ten days the remnant that has already loaded its carts sits with its oath.

The word, when it comes, is mercy with an address. “If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down; I will plant you and not uproot you, for I will relent of the disaster I have brought upon you.” The call verbs of Jeremiah's commission, completed at last on the building side. The fear underneath the Egypt plan is answered directly: “Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear; do not be afraid of him, declares the LORD, for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him.” “And I will show you compassion, and he will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land.” God even quotes their hoped-for Egypt back to them, the prayer-meeting version of it: “No, but we will go to the land of Egypt and live there, where we will not see war or hear the sound of the ram’s horn or hunger for bread.” The answer is geography-proof judgment: “then the sword you fear will overtake you there, and the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt, and you will die there.” The summary is one sentence, repeated as a verdict: the LORD has told you, O remnant of Judah, “Do not go to Egypt.” “Know for sure that I have warned you today!”

Jeremiah does not leave the delivery there. He closes by telling them what they have done: “For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God,” asking for a word they had no intention of obeying if it crossed them. “For I have told you today, but you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in all He has sent me to tell you.” “Now therefore, know for sure that by sword and famine and plague you will die in the place where you desire to go to reside.” The remnant's answer comes the moment he finishes, from Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the arrogant men: “You are lying!” They claim God never sent him to say, “You must not go to Egypt to reside there.” And their theory of the sermon names the scribe: “Rather, Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us to deliver us into the hands of the Chaldeans, so that they may put us to death or exile us to Babylon!” Baruch, who wrote down forty years of sermons at dictation, is accused of authoring the one sermon they dislike. Johanan and the commanders take the whole remnant, the men, women, children, the king's daughters, everyone Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah, and Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah with them, by force of disobedience, into Egypt. “So they entered the land of Egypt because they did not obey the voice of the LORD, and they went as far as Tahpanhes.”

At Tahpanhes the word follows them, in a sign act performed in front of Pharaoh's palace. Jeremiah, in the sight of the Jews, buries large stones in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to the palace. “I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and I will set his throne over these stones that I have embedded, and he will spread his royal pavilion over them.” Egypt's temples will burn, its gods be carried off, its sacred pillars of the temple of the sun demolished. “So he will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and he will depart from there unscathed.” “He will demolish the sacred pillars of the temple of the sun in the land of Egypt, and he will burn down the temples of the gods of Egypt.” The refuge is already annexed in prophecy. There is no Egypt-shaped hole in the word of God for this remnant to hide in.

In Egypt, Jeremiah preaches his last recorded sermon, to all the Jews in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros, and it is a review of everything they have seen: the prophets sent again and again saying, “Do not do this detestable thing that I hate,” the refusal, the burning of Jerusalem. Now they are rebuilding the same altars on Egyptian soil. “Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves by cutting off from Judah man and woman, child and infant, leaving yourselves without a remnant?” God's face, He says, is set “to bring disaster and to cut off all Judah,” and of the remnant in Egypt, “none will return except a few fugitives.” It is the sermon of a man who expects, for the first time in his life, a direct public answer.

He gets one. The men who knew their wives were burning incense to other gods, and all the women standing by, a great assembly, answer Jeremiah together: “As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you!” “Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do: We will burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and offer drink offerings to her, just as we, our fathers, our kings, and our officials did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster.” “But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine.” They have run the numbers, and their numbers acquit the Queen of Heaven and indict the years of reform. The women add their own correction to the record: “Moreover,” said the women, “when we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands’ knowledge that we made sacrificial cakes in her image and poured out drink offerings to her?” The cakes were baked in her image, in the open, with the husbands' knowledge. It is the frank confession Judah never made in Jerusalem, made at last in Egypt, in defense of the sin itself.

Jeremiah's rebuttal is a question about memory: “As for the incense you burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem,” you and your fathers, your kings and officials and the people of the land, “did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?” “So the LORD could no longer endure the evil deeds and detestable acts you committed, and your land became a desolation, a horror, and an object of cursing, without inhabitant, as it is this day.” The very incense they credit with their prosperity is the incense God remembered when He emptied the land. Then God releases them to their vow with terrible courtesy: “Go ahead, then, do what you have promised! Keep your vows!” And He swears His own counter-oath, that no man of Judah in Egypt will ever again swear by His name. “I am watching over them for harm and not for good,” He says, the watching of the almond branch turned to a single purpose. “Those who escape the sword will return from Egypt to Judah, few in number, and the whole remnant of Judah who went to dwell in the land of Egypt will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs.” The sign of it will be Pharaoh Hophra himself, delivered into his enemies' hands as Zedekiah was. The prophet's record ends there, in an Egypt he told them not to enter, carried there by the remnant he told to stay: the last congregation of his life announces, in assembly, that it will not listen, and he answers it to the end.

title: A Word for Baruch
subtitle: Jeremiah 45
description: The book's smallest chapter answers its scribe: do not seek great things for yourself; your life will be granted you as a spoil of war.
paragraphs: The smallest chapter in the book is a personal one, and the book places it out of its own time. The word was spoken in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when Baruch was writing the first scroll at Jeremiah's dictation, decades before the fall. The book sets it here instead, after Egypt, at the end of the prophet's recorded words to his own people, as if Baruch's consolation were meant to be read in the ruins it predicts. Baruch son of Neriah has been the second pair of hands on this book since the scroll: he writes what Jeremiah dictates, carries the deeds of purchase in the courtyard, reads the sermons aloud where Jeremiah cannot go, hides with him from the king, and is finally carried to Egypt as the accused author of a sermon he only transcribed. This chapter is God's one direct address to him.

What God quotes back to Baruch is Baruch's own complaint, and it sounds like his master's confessions in a quieter key: “Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain! I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest.” Jeremiah had charged God with making his pain unending and becoming like a mirage. Baruch, who has spent his working life writing down another man's sorrows on top of his own, is worn out with groaning. God does not dispute the account. His answer zooms out to the whole landscape of the age before it lands on the scribe: “Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted.” The demolition Baruch has been transcribing is God's own work on God's own building. Nobody inside it gets a private exemption from the era.

Then comes the sentence the chapter exists to carry: “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking! For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD, but wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.” Great things are not denied Baruch because he is unworthy of them. They are denied because the world in which great things are had is being dismantled, and ambition inside a demolition is a misunderstanding of the times. What God offers instead is the smallest and most durable promise in this book: his life. Not position, not vindication, not even rest. His life, granted, portable, “wherever you go.” Baruch will go many places he did not choose: into hiding from Jehoiakim, into the courtyard audiences as the prophet's hands, into Egypt against the counsel he himself wrote down. The promise has no address because the man will have no fixed one.

The phrase lands where the book has been aiming it. Life like a spoil of war was first offered to any citizen of Jerusalem who would surrender and walk out of the gates. It was spoken again to the defenders in the last days. It was paid by name to Ebed-melech the Cushite, who trusted God and padded the ropes. Now it is given to Baruch, the last of the four. The scribe who wrote “he will retain his life like a spoil of war” for strangers learns that the sentence was also addressed to him. In a book where kings get donkey burials and enrollments as childless, the scribe gets survival, and the text treats survival as a grant from God worth recording beside the oracles against nations.

The chapter is five verses long, and nothing in it suggests Baruch's life got easier after receiving it. He is still accused, still carried off, still writing. The word for Baruch is not a rescue. It is a scale for measuring every ambition that rises in a collapsing world: the greatest thing available to a faithful man in such a time may be to come through it alive, with his work done, and the book he carried intact. Baruch carried it. The words of Jeremiah that reached Egypt, and every reader since, reached them substantially through his hands.

title: Carchemish and the Coast
subtitle: Jeremiah 46-47
description: The nations section opens: Egypt routed at Carchemish is sent to Gilead for a balm that cannot heal her, and the sword is addressed over the Philistine coast.
paragraphs: After Baruch's chapter, the book opens its last great section: the word of the LORD about the nations. The first oracle concerns Egypt, and it is dated to the battle that decided the age, Carchemish on the Euphrates, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, where Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Neco's army. The oracle opens inside the Egyptian camp, in the voice of its own preparations. “Deploy your shields, small and large; advance for battle!” “Harness the horses; mount the steeds; take your positions with helmets on! Polish your spears; put on armor!” Then the camera of the sermon swings to God's view of the same army: “Why am I seeing this? They are terrified, they are retreating; their warriors are defeated, they flee in haste without looking back; terror is on every side!” Terror on every side is Jeremiah's own coinage, the name he gave Pashhur, and now it is the weather over Egypt's retreat. “The swift cannot flee, and the warrior cannot escape! In the north by the River Euphrates they stumble and fall.”

Egypt's self-image is quoted before it drowns. Rising like the Nile in flood, its waters churning, the nation boasts: “I will rise and cover the earth; I will destroy the cities and their people.” God's answer reframes the battle as liturgy. “For that day belongs to the Lord GOD of Hosts, a day of vengeance against His foes. The sword will devour until it is satisfied, until it is quenched with their blood. For the Lord GOD of Hosts will hold a sacrifice in the land of the north by the River Euphrates.” Carchemish is not a border clash in this telling. It is an altar. And then the balm of Gilead appears in the book for the last time, offered to the wrong patient as a taunt: “Go up to Gilead for balm, O Virgin Daughter of Egypt! In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing.” The wound of God's own daughter got a physician in the end. Egypt's wound, self-inflicted by pride, gets a prescription that cannot work.

A second oracle follows Nebuchadnezzar home to Egypt itself, announced in Migdol, Memphis, and Tahpanhes, the very towns where Jeremiah's remnant is hiding as he preaches it elsewhere in this book. Egypt's warriors stumble over one another and urge each other home, away from the sword of the oppressor, and their verdict on their own king is preserved: “Pharaoh king of Egypt was all noise; he has let the appointed time pass him by.” The orders to the population are the orders Judah heard: “Pack your bags for exile, O daughter dwelling in Egypt! For Memphis will be laid waste, destroyed and uninhabited.” “Egypt is a beautiful heifer, but a gadfly from the north is coming against her.” Her mercenaries are fattened calves who will turn and flee together; she will hiss like a fleeing serpent before the woodsmen. “They will chop down her forest, declares the LORD, dense though it may be, for they are more numerous than locusts; they cannot be counted.” Even Egypt's god is on the charge sheet: “Behold, I am about to punish Amon god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh, Egypt with her gods and kings, and those who trust in Pharaoh.” And then, in the middle of the sack of Egypt, the limit that keeps ending these oracles: “But after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old, declares the LORD.”

The Egypt oracle closes, remarkably, by talking to Jacob. “But you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed, O Israel. For I will surely save you out of a distant place, your descendants from the land of their captivity!” And the distinction that governs the whole nations section is stated to Israel inside Egypt's judgment: “Though I will completely destroy all the nations to which I have banished you, I will not completely destroy you. Yet I will discipline you justly, and will by no means leave you unpunished.” It is the consolation's own sentence, read aloud over Carchemish, so that nobody mistakes the nations' ruin for Israel's: the rod is destroyed completely; the son is disciplined justly.

The second oracle is the shortest in the section, seven verses against the Philistines, dated before Pharaoh struck down Gaza. Its image is water again, but from the wrong direction for a coastal people: “See how the waters are rising from the north and becoming an overflowing torrent. They will overflow the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants.” The sound arrives before the army: “at the sound of the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels. The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp.” Fathers not turning back for their sons is the panic's measure. “For the day has come to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every remaining ally.” Gaza shaves her head in mourning. “The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning; Ashkelon will be silenced.” And the oracle ends in a dialogue with the weapon itself, the only speech of its kind in the book: “Alas, O sword of the LORD, how long until you rest? Return to your sheath; cease and be still!” “How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it? He has appointed it against Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland.” Even the sword would stop if it could. It cannot, because it was appointed, and appointments in this book are kept.

title: Moab, Settled on Its Dregs
subtitle: Jeremiah 48
description: Moab, settled like wine on its dregs and never poured out, is poured at last, and God Himself wails over the nation He is judging.
paragraphs: The Moab oracle is the longest in the nations section before Babylon, and it begins with the map being erased town by town: woe to Nebo, Kiriathaim captured, the fortress shattered, Madmen silenced. In Heshbon the enemy council devises the plan in words: “Come, let us cut her off from nationhood.” From Horonaim a voice cries out, “Devastation and great destruction!” and the road fills with weeping, up the ascent to Luhith and down to Horonaim, a whole nation on the move with its little ones crying out. “Flee! Run for your lives! Become like a juniper in the desert.” The charge beneath the invasion is trust in the wrong reserves: “Because you trust in your works and treasures, you too will be captured, and Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials.” Moab's god will be deported with his clergy, a refugee deity, in the world Jeremiah has been describing all along.

One verse explains why Moab's judgment takes the shape it does, and it is a winemaker's image. God even curses reluctance in the executioners: “Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed.” Then the diagnosis: “Moab has been at ease from youth, settled like wine on its dregs; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel or gone into exile. So his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged.” Judah was poured out through exile after exile; Moab was never disturbed, never decanted, never disciplined, and so Moab arrives at old age tasting exactly as he did in youth, pride and all. The remedy is the pouring itself: “Therefore behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will send to him wanderers, who will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars.” After it, Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, the oracle says, as Israel was ashamed of Bethel. Shame, in this book, is what exile is for.

The boasting is quoted so the breaking can be measured against it. Moab's warriors announce themselves: “We are warriors, mighty men ready for battle.” The neighbors are instructed to take up the public mourning: “Mourn for him, all you who surround him, everyone who knows his name,” and report the damage in the formula of state funerals: “The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken.” The drunkenness Moab poured for others returns: “Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD; so Moab will wallow in his own vomit, and he will also become a laughingstock.” His specific cruelty is named: “Was not Israel your object of ridicule? Was he ever found among thieves? For whenever you speak of him you shake your head.” The head-shaking spectator at Israel's disaster is sentenced to be the spectacle. The proud are told to go live like birds: “Abandon the towns and settle among the rocks, O dwellers of Moab! Be like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave.” And the file on his character is read aloud: “We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit, his proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart.”

Then, in the middle of Moab's judgment, God's own voice breaks in the opposite direction, and it is the most unexpected sound in the nations section. “Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab; I will moan for the men of Kir-heres.” “I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah, more than I weep for Jazer.” The judge laments the judged. “Therefore My heart laments like a flute for Moab; it laments like a flute for the men of Kir-heres, because the wealth they acquired has perished.” Every head shaved, every beard clipped, every hand gashed, sackcloth on every waist, because “I have shattered Moab like an unwanted jar,” the potter's imagery of the whole book surfacing once more over a foreign nation. An eagle spreads its wings over Moab. “Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab,” and flight only shuffles a man from one to the next. “Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished; for your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.”

And after forty-six verses of it, the last verse reverses the door. “Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,” declares the LORD. The oracle then signs its own certificate, the only one in the section to do so: “Here ends the judgment on Moab.” Ends is the operative word. The judgment on Moab has an end date written into its last line, exile and restoration both, and the nation that was never poured gets poured at last, and then, in the latter days, gathered. Moab's story in Jeremiah does not finish with the eagle or the jar. It finishes with captivity itself reversed, in a sentence set down by the same prophet who recorded the shattering.

title: Milcom, Esau, and the Small Nations
subtitle: Jeremiah 49
description: Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Elam are judged in one chapter; two of the five end with restoration, and Edom does not.
paragraphs: Chapter 49 gathers five shorter oracles, and the first is a lawsuit over an inheritance. “Has Israel no sons? Is he without heir? Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?” While Judah was falling, Ammon's god had moved into the territory of Gad east of the Jordan, and Ammon's people had settled in its cities. God's answer is a reversal of occupancy: the battle cry will sound against Rabbah, the capital will become a heap of ruins, and “Then Israel will drive out their dispossessors, says the LORD.” Milcom himself will be deported, as Chemosh was: “Milcom will go into exile together with his priests and officials.” Ammon's self-confidence is quoted in one short sentence from the faithless daughter who trusts in her riches: “Who can come against me?” The answer is terror from all those around her, each fugitive driven headlong with no one to regather them. And then the door the section keeps leaving open: “Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity.” Ammon's oracle ends in restoration. Edom's will not.

Edom's oracle opens as an obituary for famous wisdom. “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom decayed?” The dwellers of Dedan are told to turn and run and lie low, because God is bringing disaster on Esau himself. The thoroughness of it is measured against ordinary plunder: “If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleanings? Were thieves to come in the night, would they not steal only what they wanted?” “But I will strip Esau bare; I will uncover his hiding places, and he will be unable to conceal himself.” Thieves and harvesters leave a remainder. This judgment leaves none, his descendants destroyed with his relatives and neighbors. And in the middle of it stands one of the strangest mercies in the book, spoken over Edom's most helpless: “Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me.” Then the cup argument closes the case. Edom had watched Judah drink from the cup of wrath and counted itself exempt: “If those who do not deserve to drink the cup must drink it, can you possibly remain unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too.”

Edom's pride is altitude. “The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks, O occupiers of the mountain summit.” “Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down.” Bozrah will become a desolation and a curse, her cities in ruins forever, measured by the oldest yardstick of total judgment: “As Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown along with their neighbors,” says the LORD, “no one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” The executioner arrives in the image that will close this chapter's Babylon oracle two chapters later: “Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture. For in an instant I will chase Edom from her land.” Behind the sentence stands a challenge no shepherd has ever answered: “For who is like Me, and who can challenge Me? What shepherd can stand against Me?” Edom gets a second, fuller telling later in this series in Obadiah's own book, at the fall; this is Jeremiah's, told whole here and never stitched to it.

Damascus hears a bad report and comes apart before a blow lands. “Hamath and Arpad are put to shame, for they have heard a bad report; they are agitated like the sea; their anxiety cannot be calmed.” The city of praise turns to flee, her young men marked for the streets and her warriors for silence, and God's sentence is fire: “I will set fire to the walls of Damascus; it will consume the fortresses of Ben-hadad.” Kedar and Hazor, the tent peoples of the east, are next, a nation with no walls to breach: their tents, flocks, curtains, and camels are the plunder, and the cry raised over them is Jeremiah's own phrase turned outward: “Terror is on every side!” Their security was the absence of everything Babylon usually has to break: “Rise up, advance against a nation at ease, one that dwells securely.” “They have no gates or bars; they live alone.” It does not save them. “Hazor will become a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever. No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.”

Elam's oracle is the only one in the chapter dated like a sermon, to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, years before the fall it belongs beside. Elam is an archer nation, and the sentence strikes the weapon first: “Behold, I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might.” The four winds will scatter its people until there is no nation without Elamite exiles in it, and God announces a throne transplanted into the enemy's capital: “I will set My throne in Elam, and destroy its king and officials.” Then the last line reverses it: “Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity.” Set the chapter's endings side by side and a pattern the outline of this book keeps showing comes into focus. Ammon ends restored. Elam ends restored. Moab, in the chapter before, ends restored. Edom does not. Neither, in the chapters ahead, does Babylon. The nearer neighbors who mocked and grabbed land are sentenced to exile with a return written into the sentence. Esau and the great empire are sentenced without one, and Jeremiah lets the difference stand without explaining it.

title: Babylon Is Captured
subtitle: Jeremiah 50
description: The banner is lifted and nothing held back: Babylon is captured, Bel is shamed, and Israel and Judah come weeping together to ask the way to Zion.
paragraphs: The Babylon oracle is announced like a headline to be published everywhere at once: a banner lifted, nothing held back. “Babylon is captured; Bel is put to shame; Marduk is shattered, her images are disgraced, her idols are broken in pieces.” A nation from the north will make her land a desolation where neither man nor beast remains. But woven directly into the capture announcement, before any siege detail, comes the return. “In those days and at that time, declares the LORD, the children of Israel and the children of Judah will come together, weeping as they come, and will seek the LORD their God.” North and south together, weeping on the road: “They will ask the way to Zion and turn their faces toward it. They will come and join themselves to the LORD in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.” Babylon's fall and Israel's homecoming are not two prophecies. They are one event seen from its two ends.

The flock theology of the whole book is gathered into a few verses. “My people are lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray, causing them to roam the mountains. They have wandered from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.” Those who found the straying sheep devoured them and excused themselves in words preserved on the record: “We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their true pasture, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.” God's answer to the excuse is an evacuation order for His own people: “Flee from the midst of Babylon; depart from the land of the Chaldeans; be like the he-goats that lead the flock.” And the sentence on the devourers runs on the book's oldest arithmetic: “Since this is the vengeance of the LORD, take out your vengeance upon her; as she has done, do the same to her.”

The devouring is given a two-act history. “Israel is a scattered flock, chased away by lions. The first to devour him was the king of Assyria; the last to crush his bones was Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.” Therefore: “I will punish the king of Babylon and his land as I punished the king of Assyria.” Assyria's punishment is the precedent and the pattern, already visible in history for anyone who wants to check. Israel will be returned to his pasture to graze on Carmel and Bashan, his soul satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and Gilead. Then comes the sentence that overturns every record office in the ancient world: “In those days and at that time, declares the LORD, a search will be made for Israel’s guilt, but there will be none, and for Judah’s sins, but they will not be found; for I will forgive the remnant I preserve.” The guilt Jeremiah spent forty years itemizing will be searched for in those days like a missing document, and not found, because God will have forgiven the remnant He preserves.

Babylon is addressed as broken equipment and a trapped animal. “How the hammer of the whole earth lies broken and shattered! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” “I laid a snare for you, O Babylon, and you were caught before you knew it. You were found and captured because you challenged the LORD.” Fugitives arriving in Zion will declare there “the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple,” and the burned temple stands behind this whole oracle as its warrant. God's address to the empire is personal: “Behold, I am against you, O arrogant one,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts, “for your day has come, the time when I will punish you.” The arrogant one will stumble and fall with no one to pick him up, and fire will go out through his cities.

The ground of it all is stated as a courtroom fact. The sons of Israel and Judah are oppressed together, their captors holding them fast and refusing release: “Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name. He will fervently plead their case so that He may bring rest to the earth, but turmoil to those who live in Babylon.” Then the sword is addressed down Babylon's whole hierarchy like a roll call: “A sword is against the Chaldeans, declares the LORD, against those who live in Babylon, and against her officials and wise men.” A sword against her false prophets, her warriors, her horses and chariots, her treasuries. “A drought is upon her waters, and they will be dried up. For it is a land of graven images, and the people go mad over idols.” Desert creatures and hyenas will live in her ruins, uninhabited from generation to generation, measured by Sodom's measure. And at the end the oracle reaches back to chapter 49 and takes up the lion oracle spoken over Edom, word for word, and aims it at the greater prey: “Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture. For in an instant I will chase Babylon from her land.” The plans drawn up against Teman are drawn up again against the empire, and the last sound of the chapter is geological: at the sound of Babylon's capture, the earth will quake, and a cry will be heard among the nations.

title: The War Club
subtitle: Jeremiah 51:1-35
description: God addresses His war club, sings the Creator hymn over Babylon a second time, and hears Zion's complaint entered into the record.
paragraphs: Chapter 51 opens the second half of the Babylon oracle with a destroyer's wind stirred up against Babylon and the people of Leb-kamai, strangers sent to winnow her and empty her land. Before the winnowing is described, the oracle stops to say what Babylon's fall does not mean: “For Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, the LORD of Hosts, though their land is full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel.” The guilt is admitted in the same breath as the loyalty. Then the evacuation order goes out again, urgent as ever: “Flee from Babylon! Escape with your lives! Do not be destroyed in her punishment. For this is the time of the LORD’s vengeance; He will pay her what she deserves.” Babylon's whole career is summed in one object: “Babylon was a gold cup in the hand of the LORD, making the whole earth drunk. The nations drank her wine; therefore the nations have gone mad.” The cup that passed from nation to nation through Jeremiah's sermons is itself about to be emptied and broken.

The balm of this book makes its last appearance here, over Babylon's wound. “Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been shattered. Wail for her; get her balm for her pain; perhaps she can be healed.” The physicians answer in their own voice, and it is a resignation letter: “We tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed. Abandon her! Let each of us go to his own land, for her judgment extends to the sky and reaches to the clouds.” Gilead's balm could not heal Egypt, and no remedy on earth heals Babylon, whose judgment has outgrown the sky the physicians measure by. Israel's voice answers theirs with the opposite report: “The LORD has brought forth our vindication; come, let us tell in Zion what the LORD our God has accomplished.” Then the agents of the fall are named: the LORD has aroused the spirit of the kings of the Medes, “because His plan is aimed at Babylon to destroy her, for it is the vengeance of the LORD,” and Jeremiah gives the reason its full weight in four words, “vengeance for His temple.”

To the city herself the sentence is a tailor's image: “You who dwell by many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come; the thread of your life is cut.” Then the oracle pauses the destruction to sing. The Creator hymn from the sermon against idols in chapter 10 is read aloud a second time over Babylon: the LORD who made the earth by His power, who thunders and gathers the clouds, beside whom every goldsmith is shamed by his breathless images. Its closing line is carried over whole: “The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things, and of the tribe of His inheritance,” and the name is given its own sentence, “the LORD of Hosts is His name.” Babylon falls inside a world somebody made, and the hymn says who.

Then God turns and addresses His own weapon, unnamed in the address itself, in the most relentless cadence of the chapter: “You are My war club, My weapon for battle. With you I shatter nations; with you I bring kingdoms to ruin.” The series runs down the whole of Babylon's world: horse and rider, chariot and driver, man and woman, old man and youth, young man and maiden, shepherd and flock, farmer and oxen, governors and officials, each shattered with the same instrument. The purpose is stated to Babylon's face: “Before your very eyes I will repay Babylon and all the dwellers of Chaldea for all the evil they have done in Zion.” And the empire is renamed for the occasion: “Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, you who devastate the whole earth, declares the LORD. I will stretch out My hand against you; I will roll you over the cliffs and turn you into a charred mountain.” “No one shall retrieve from you a cornerstone or a foundation stone, because you will become desolate forever.” The mountain that crushed nations will not yield so much as a reusable stone.

The summons goes out across the north: Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz called up, captains appointed, horses like swarming locusts, the kings of the Medes with all the lands they rule. Inside the city, the defense dissolves before it fights. “The warriors of Babylon have stopped fighting; they sit in their strongholds. Their strength is exhausted; they have become like women. Babylon’s homes have been set ablaze, the bars of her gates are broken.” The news outruns the king's ability to hear it: “One courier races to meet another, and messenger follows messenger, to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end.” The fords are seized, the marshes fired, the soldiers terrified. Babylon is reclassified as an agricultural surface awaiting its season: “The Daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time it is trampled. In just a little while her harvest time will come.” And the half-chapter closes in the voice of the victim herself, Zion speaking her evidence into the record: “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me. He has set me aside like an empty vessel; he has swallowed me like a monster; he filled his belly with my delicacies and vomited me out.” “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon,” says the dweller of Zion. “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea,” says Jerusalem. The war club is God's. The complaint is Jerusalem's. Both are on the record before the sentence is carried out.

title: The Scroll in the Euphrates
subtitle: Jeremiah 51:36-64
description: God pleads Zion's case, Bel is made to spew out what he swallowed, and Seraiah sinks the Babylon scroll in the Euphrates on a stone.
paragraphs: God answers Zion's complaint in the language of a retained advocate, the Redeemer's pledge from the chapter before now spoken as a verdict: “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf; I will dry up her sea and make her springs run dry.” The sentence that follows is total and quiet: “Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals, an object of horror and scorn, without inhabitant.” Her princes will roar together like young lions and growl like cubs, and God will host the last feast of the empire Himself: “While they are flushed with heat, I will serve them a feast, and I will make them drunk so that they may revel; then they will fall asleep forever and never wake up, declares the LORD.” Down they go like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with male goats, the warlords of the world processed as livestock.

Then the oracle uses Babylon's secret name: “How Sheshach has been captured! The praise of all the earth has been seized. What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” Sheshach is Babylon's name in cipher, the same cipher name that closed the cup sermon years before, when the king of Sheshach was told he would drink last of all. The sea comes up over her and covers her in turbulent waves; her cities become a dry land where no son of man passes through. Even Bel, who swallowed the temple vessels and the nations' worship, will be made to give it back: “I will punish Bel in Babylon. I will make him spew out what he swallowed. The nations will no longer stream to him; even the wall of Babylon will fall.” And through the middle of the sentence on the city runs the standing order to God's people inside it: “Come out of her, My people! Save your lives, each of you, from the fierce anger of the LORD.”

The oracle even prepares the exiles for the waiting. Rumors will come one year and then another the next, violence in the land and ruler against ruler, and they are told not to let their hearts faint at the noise. Heaven and earth will shout for joy when the destroyers come from the north. To those already out, the word is movement and memory: “You who have escaped the sword, depart and do not linger! Remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind.” The exiles answer in the oracle with their shame spoken aloud: “We are ashamed because we have heard reproach; disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the LORD’s house.” No height rescues the city from the sentence: “Even if Babylon ascends to the heavens and fortifies her lofty stronghold, the destroyers I send will come against her.” The ground is named without decoration: “for the LORD is a God of retribution; He will repay in full.”

The feast sentence is repeated for the leadership by rank: “I will make her princes and wise men drunk, along with her governors, officials, and warriors. Then they will fall asleep forever and not wake up,” declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts. The engineering gets its own verse: “Babylon’s thick walls will be leveled, and her high gates consumed by fire. So the labor of the people will be for nothing; the nations will exhaust themselves to fuel the flames.” And then the oracle leaves the page and becomes an errand. Jeremiah gives the message to Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, the quartermaster, who is traveling to Babylon with King Zedekiah in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign, while Babylon still rules the world and Zedekiah still wears a crown. Seraiah is Baruch's brother. The scribe's family carries this book's most dangerous deliveries. Jeremiah has written on a single scroll all the disaster that will come upon Babylon, all these words, and Seraiah is to read them aloud when he arrives, and then pray God's own promise back to Him: “O LORD, You have promised to cut off this place so that no one will remain,” neither man nor beast; “Indeed, it will be desolate forever.”

When the reading is finished, Seraiah is to tie a stone to the scroll and cast it into the Euphrates, and say: “In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again, because of the disaster I will bring upon her. And her people will grow weary.” It is the book's last sign act, performed in the enemy's capital by an officer of a vassal king, years before anyone in Babylon had reason to tremble. Jeremiah's first scroll was burned by a king and rewritten by a scribe, with many similar words added, and it survived. This scroll is sunk on purpose by the prophet's own order, and it survives too, because its words were copied into the book before the stone was tied. “Here end the words of Jeremiah.” The sentence sits at the bottom of the river with the scroll, and it is not the end of the book. One chapter remains, and it belongs to the record keepers.

title: Jehoiachin at the King's Table
subtitle: Jeremiah 52
description: The appendix retells the fall as record, counts the exile by name and number, and ends on a pardoned king dining at Babylon's table for life.
paragraphs: “The words of Jeremiah” have ended, and the book closes with an appendix of record, the fall of Jerusalem told once more from Jeremiah's side. The Kings account of these events stands earlier in this series, told whole there; this telling is set beside it, not stitched into it. It begins with the last king. Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem; his mother's name was Hamutal of Libnah. He did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done, and the chapter gives the reason the whole story happened in one line: it was because of the anger of the LORD, “until He finally banished them from His presence.” Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. In the ninth year of his reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar marched against Jerusalem with his entire army, encamped outside the city, and built a siege wall all around it. The city was kept under siege until the eleventh year. By the ninth day of the fourth month the famine was so severe that the people of the land had no food. That night the city was breached, and the men of war fled by the gate between the two walls near the king's garden, heading toward the Arabah. The Chaldeans pursued and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army deserted him.

At Riblah in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon pronounced judgment. There the sons of Zedekiah were slaughtered before his eyes, and all the officials of Judah were killed. Then Zedekiah's eyes were put out, he was bound with bronze shackles, and he was taken to Babylon and kept in custody until his dying day, the last sight of his life the death of his sons. On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan captain of the guard entered Jerusalem. He burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem, every significant building, and the Chaldean army broke down all the walls around the city. Nebuzaradan carried into exile some of the poorest people and those who remained, the deserters who had defected, and the rest of the craftsmen. But he left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields: the same poor of the land who gathered that summer around Gedaliah at Mizpah, in the chapters this book has already told.

The record lingers over the bronze, the way an inventory lingers over what cannot be replaced. The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD and carried all the bronze to Babylon: the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and every article of bronze used in the temple service; and the captain took the basins, censers, lampstands, pans, and drink offering bowls, anything made of pure gold or fine silver. As for the two pillars, the Sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it, and the stands Solomon had made, “the weight of the bronze from all these articles was beyond measure.” Each pillar was eighteen cubits tall and twelve cubits in circumference, hollow, four fingers thick, with a capital five cubits high and a network of pomegranates all around, ninety-six pomegranates on the sides of each capital and a hundred in all above the network. Solomon's craftsmanship is measured one last time on its way to the scrap carts.

The people are inventoried with the same care. The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest of second rank, and the three doorkeepers. The Zephaniah named here is the priest who carried Zedekiah's secret questions to Jeremiah through the last years; the Seraiah named here is the chief priest, not Baruch's brother the quartermaster who sank the scroll. From the city he took a court official appointed over the men of war, seven trusted royal advisers, the scribe of the captain of the army who had enlisted the people of the land, and sixty men found in the city. Nebuzaradan brought them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and there they were struck down and put to death. “So Judah was taken into exile, away from its own land.” Then the appendix counts the exile itself, by the king of Babylon's regnal years: in the seventh year, 3,023 Jews; in the eighteenth year, 832 people from Jerusalem; in the twenty-third year, 745 Jews. In all, 4,600 people were taken away. The book that began with a boy's call ends its record with arithmetic.

And then, after the arithmetic, one more entry, dated thirty-seven years into Jehoiachin's exile. On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of that year, in the first year of the reign of Evil-merodach king of Babylon, the new king pardoned Jehoiachin king of Judah and released him from prison. “And he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and set his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.” “So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life.” The king of Babylon provided him a daily portion, every day of his life, until the day of his death. It is the same final scene the Kings record ends on, and Jeremiah's book chooses it too: not the breach, not the fire, not the bronze on the carts, but a son of David out of prison clothes, seated above the other captive kings, eating at the table of Babylon for the rest of his life. The line Jeremiah traced through Jeconiah's curse and the signet ring promise is still alive in exile, fed daily. On that small, stubborn mercy, the largest book of the prophets closes.
